paper_title: From Fragmentation to Fusion: A Survey and Roadmap for Omnimodal Embeddings

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Embedding models underpin virtually every modern AI system, from search engines to recommendation systems. Despite shared mathematical foundations, research on embedding models remains fragmented by modality: the communities develop largely in isolation, seldom exchanging insights. We argue that this fragmentation obscures a deeper convergence. Driven by contrastive learning, Transformer architectures, and a granularity shift, embedding research across modalities is converging toward a common set of principles, even as modality-specific challenges remain underexplored. To reason across this convergence without conflating it, we propose a framework of three progressively harder capabilities: coverage, comparability, and compositionality. Three paths toward unification satisfy these in turn: transformation broadens coverage, alignment enables comparability, and joint embedding, the terminus we advocate, aims at compositionality. This position paper traces the resulting evolution, providing the first unified, cross-cutting treatment of omnimodal embedding research.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: At the heart of modern machine learning lies deceptively simple idea: map complex, unstructured data into vector space where geometric relationships carry semantic meaning. An embedding model is function fθ : Rd that transforms an input drawn from some data domain (e.g., sentence, an image, sound wave, molecular graph, time series) into d-dimensional vector = fθ(x), such that the relative positions of vectors reflect the semantic relationships among inputs. When this map is well-learned, semantically similar inputs cluster together while dissimilar ones are pushed apart, enabling efficient nearest-neighbor search, clustering, classification, and cross-modal alignment through simple vector operations. The ubiquity of embedding models is striking: in information retrieval dense embeddings have largely replaced sparse bag-of-words representations like BM25 (Robertson & Zaragoza, 2009) to enable semantic search (Karpukhin et al., 2020; Izacard et al., 2022); in recommendation, learned item embeddings power web-scale retrieval and ranking; and in cross-modal settings, aligned embedding spacespopularized at web scale by CLIP (Radford et al., 2021) and CLAP (Elizalde et al., 2023)let us search images with text and describe audio with language. Despite this central role, the study of embedding models has been fragmented along modality boundaries. We argue that this fragmentation is the central obstacle to progress, and that it runs deeper than is usually acknowledged, manifesting on three interlocking levels: in research, in surveys, and in evaluation. 1.1 The Fragmentation Problem: Silos of Research, Surveys, and Evaluation What counts as modality? Our unit of analysis is the coarse modality family: text and code, image and video, audio, graph, table, and time series. The fragmentation we diagnose lives at family level: it is communities, venues, and benchmarks that are siloed, and it is at that level that convergence must be measured. In contrast, modality counts in the literature may also include intra-family derivativesviews and channels of single underlying object produced by signal processing or annotation. As an example, 4M-21 (Bachmann et al., 2024) claims to cover twenty-one modalities, yet almost all of them (such as depth, segmentation, edges, human pose, and feature maps) are views of the same visual scenes. In our taxonomy they are not counted as peer modalities, but derived views within the vision family (refer to Table 6 in Section 9 for details). Research silos. Text embedding research (Gao et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2022a; Su et al., 2023; Lee et al., 2025a) has evolved largely independently of vision embedding research (Caron et al., 2021; He et al., 2022), audio self-supervised learning (Baevski et al., 2020; Hsu et al., 2021), graph representation learning (Bordes et al., 2013; Grover & Leskovec, 2016; Khoshraftar & An, 2024), time-series embeddings (Yue et al., 2022; Nie et al., 2023), and table representation learning (Yin et al., 2020; Herzig et al., 2020; Deng et al., 2020). Each community holds its own workshops, releases its own checkpoints, and optimizes its own benchmarks; methods that would be ported straightforwardly within one literature are repeatedly reinvented from scratch in another, and the connections between them go unnamed. Survey silos. This research-level fragmentation is faithfully mirrored in the survey literature. We have excellent monolithic reviews of single modalities: text embedding surveys (Nie et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025b), vision self-supervised reviews (Uelwer et al., 2023), speech representation surveys (Mohamed et al., 2022), graph embedding reviews (Khoshraftar & An, 2024), and tabular representation reviews (Jiang et al., 2026). These surveys are invaluable within their fields, but 4 Omnimodal Embeddings they are themselves evidence of the fragmentation: they almost never cross the modality boundary to systematically compare and connect the core methodologies of sibling communities. graphembedding survey may discuss view augmentation at length without ever observing that texts SimCSE achieves implicit positive pair construction through dropout (Gao et al., 2021); vision survey may extol masked autoencoding without noting that audio arrived at the same principle year apart (Baevski et al., 2020; Hsu et al., 2021; Huang et al., 2022a). Each survey charts its own domain; none builds the bridges between them. Evaluation silos. Finally, the fragmentation reaches evaluation. Text, code, audio, and vision have each matured their own frozen-encoder benchmarkMTEB and its multilingual extension MMTEB for text (Muennighoff et al., 2023; Enevoldsen et al., 2025), CoIR for code (Li et al., 2025e), SUPERB and its successors for audio (Yang et al., 2021; Turian et al., 2021; Yuan et al., 2023; Heigold et al., 2025; Assadi et al., 2026a), and retrieval/classification suites for vision (Russakovsky et al., 2015; Radenovic et al., 2018). In contrast, tables and time series are still scored mainly through task heads and prediction archives: table QA/fact-verification suites (Pasupat & Liang, 2015; Yu et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2020c), with MTEB analogs only now emerging (Vogel et al., 2026; Qiang et al., 2026), and time series classification archives (Bagnall et al., 2018; Dau et al., 2019) alongside forecasting archives (Godahewa et al., 2021). Yet, there is no single yardstick that measures how methodology (not just model) generalizes across modalities. We have islands of evaluation, but no shared sea to compare them on. This fragmentation across research, surveys, and evaluation is not an impression but measurable structure, as we quantify in Appendix B. combined analysis of 1,352 formally published embedding papers (20232025) and decade of arXiv preprints (20152025) indicates that the overwhelming majority of embedding research is single-modality, each modality publishing in its home communitys venues, while works that explicitly cross modality boundaries account for under 5% of both samples and emerge only recently. This is the core obstacleand the opportunitythis paper sets out to address. 1.2 Why Fragmentation Matters At first sight, fragmentation is an organizational complaint rather than scientific one: field can be fragmented and healthy, with each silo producing the best possible encoder for its own modality. But two independent lines of evidence suggest that embedding research cannot stop thereone from the science of intelligence, one from the trajectory of AI itself. Concepts must be grounded in more than symbols. The physical world is inherently multimodal: real-world entities and events manifest simultaneously across visual, auditory, tactile, and temporal channels, rather than existing in isolated sensory silos. Mirroring this reality, the first line of evidence is that human intelligence does not organize knowledge by modality. Meaning cannot be assembled from closed system of symbol-to-symbol mappings (Harnad, 1990): human concepts are grounded in multimodal perceptual and motor experience (Barsalou, 1999), and are organized in the brain in hub-and-spoke architecturea modality-invariant hub carrying conceptual knowledge for all modalities, flanked by modality-specific spokes (Patterson et al., 2007; Ralph et al., 2017). Rather than keeping channels isolated, human cognition fuses multisensory cues (Ernst & Banks, 2002) and bootstraps word meaning from cross-modal co-occurrence before language acquisition (Gogate & Bahrick, 1998; 2001; Smith & Yu, 2008). While language models recover some perceptual statistics from corpus co-occurrence (Abdou et al., 2021; Huh et al., 2024), text remains lossy projection of experience: it cannot supervise knowledge that is never put into words, nor provide the cross-modal consistency check that disambiguates and stabilizes concepts. representation literature fragmented by modality is, in these terms, manufacturing spokes while nobody builds the hub. Representation is falling behind generation. The second line of evidence is more recent, and more measurable. On the generative side of AI, omnimodality is deployed reality: GPT-4o has jointly consumed text, audio, image, and video within single model since May 2024 (OpenAI, 2024), and 5 Omnimodal Embeddings any-to-any generative research covers the same four natural modalities in both directions (Wu et al., 2024b). On the embedding side, breadth is achieved without fusion: pairwise-aligned spaces have spanned many modalities since ImageBind and LanguageBind (Girdhar et al., 2023; Zhu et al., 2024a; Chen et al., 2026f), but verified joint fusion (where measurable compositional gains are confirmed beyond processing inputs together) has so far been obtained only for textimage pairs (Yang et al., 2026) and partially for composed text, vision, and audio queries (Huynh et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026b). Fused omni embedding models and benchmarks covering text, image, video, and audio appeared only in late 2025 (Xiao et al., 2025a; Xu et al., 2025a; Tang et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026b; Hönicke et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2026a)almost two years after the generative side crossed the same threshold. The consequence is an asymmetry inside the very substrate on which generative AI depends: models that jointly perceive four modalities are indexed and remembered by retrieval systems that are bimodal, pairwise-aligned, or text-centric, with the retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline being the most common case. Fragmentation is not slowing peripheral subfield; it is the bottleneck of the omni stack itself. The remedy is neither to abandon the single-modality literatures nor to merely catalog them. Our contribution is not to replace the deep, expert, single-modality surveys but to provide meta-level synthesis: to build the conceptual bridges between those continents and reveal the shared principles beneath them. The synthesis is worth more than scholarly tidiness, because what joint embedding built on those principles would give is already visible in miniature: multimodal retrieval over single shared index (Wei et al., 2024a), generation grounded in retrieved images and text rather than text alone (Chen et al., 2022b; Yasunaga et al., 2023; Hu et al., 2025b), robot memory stored as text captions rather than raw experience (Anwar et al., 2025), and emergent zero-shot retrieval and composition between modalities that never co-occurred in training (Girdhar et al., 2023). Each payoff today exists only on the few modality pairs its prototype happens to span. Giving them common geometry is what the rest of this paper sets out to do. 1.3 Four Convergent Trends Looking past the silos, four trends are quietly unifying all the modalities. 1. Contrastive learning as universal objective. From InfoNCE in text (van den Oord et al., 2018; Gao et al., 2021) to CLIP in vision-language (Radford et al., 2021) and CLAP in audiolanguage (Elizalde et al., 2023), the contrastive paradigmpull positives together, push negatives aparthas become the lingua franca of representation learning across all modalities. 2. Transformers as universal encoders. The Transformer architecture (Vaswani et al., 2017) has become the default backbone across modalitiesViT for images (Dosovitskiy et al., 2021), audio Transformers for speech (Baevski et al., 2020), Graph Transformers for structured data (Yuan et al., 2026; Shehzad et al., 2026), and patch-based Transformers for time series (Nie et al., 2023). In text, decoder-only LLMs are increasingly repurposed as embedding models (Wang et al., 2024d; Lee et al., 2025a; Muennighoff et al., 2025), while multimodal LLMs are being adapted for cross-modal embedding tasks (Jiang et al., 2025; Lin et al., 2025), blurring the line between generative and representational models. 3. The pretrainfinetune paradigm. The dominant recipe has converged on two-stage pipeline: pretrain on large-scale unlabeled data with reconstructive or self-supervised objectives (MLM for text (Devlin et al., 2019), MAE for vision (He et al., 2022), masked prediction for audio (Baevski et al., 2020)), then finetune on task-specific or contrastive data. This paradigmfrom BERTs MLM followed by contrastive finetuning, to wav2vec 2.0s masked prediction followed by adaptation, to DINOs self-distillation followed by transfer (Caron et al., 2021)has proven remarkably effective regardless of input modality. 4. The granularity shift. Each modality has independently shifted from tokenor pixel-level objectives to sequenceor image-level ones: text built sentence-level contrast (Reimers & Gurevych, 2019; Gao et al., 2021) and passage-level dense retrieval (Karpukhin et al., 2020) on top of word-level skip-gram (Mikolov et al., 2013); vision pooled image-level contrast (Chen et al., 6 Omnimodal Embeddings 2020b) and patch-level masked reconstruction (He et al., 2022) into whole-image representations; graph moved from node-level skip-gram (Perozzi et al., 2014) to graph-level masked latent prediction (Skenderi et al., 2025); audio progressed from frame-level masking (Baevski et al., 2020) to utterance-level discrimination; and time series shifted from point-level classification to window/patch-level modeling (Nie et al., 2023) and series-level universal representations (Yue et al., 2022; Goswami et al., 2024). While local feature embeddings remain indispensable for fine-grained grounding and dense correspondence, this upward shift reflects shared insight: for broad retrieval and cross-modal alignment, representations are most directly comparable when they encode semantics at the level of complete semantic units rather than constituent parts. These four trends are picked up in the chapters that follow: the first becomes the trainingobjectives chapter (Section 3), the second the architecture chapter (Section 4), and the fourth the representational-object chapter (Section 5); the third (the pretrainfinetune paradigm) is folded into the objectives chapter (Section 3.4). These convergences are not coincidental. The Platonic Representation Hypothesis (Huh et al., 2024) suggests that representations across modalities may be converging toward shared statistical model of realitya platonic representation space. Empirically, Jha et al. (2025) demonstrate universal latent semantic structure across text embedding spaces, enabling unsupervised translation of embeddings from one vector space to another without paired data, with preliminary extensions toward multimodal spacesevidence that the convergence is representational, not merely architectural. Recent omni-/multi-modal embedding models such as e5-omni (Chen et al., 2026b), jina-embeddings-v5-omni (Hönicke et al., 2026), MM-Embed (Lin et al., 2025), and UniME (Gu et al., 2025) are early realizations of this vision, mapping text, image, video, and audio into shared space, whether by explicit cross-modal alignment or by fusing modalities inside single encoder. 1.4 Our Position and Roadmap Our central claim can be stated in one sentence: Embedding research is converging along shared principles (Part II), which makes it possible to proceed from transformation and alignment to true fusion (Part III); but to realize an omnimodal joint embedding we must confront each modalitys unique challenges and borrow each others hard-won techniques (Part IV). This claim, illustrated in Figure 1, organizes the paper into four parts. Part IThe Unified Foundation (Section 2) establishes modality-agnostic anatomy of embedding models (components, data units, and the exposed representational objects), and introduces the analytical lens (intersection, difference, reuse) used throughout this paper. Part IIConvergent Principles (Sections 3 to 5) makes the case for convergence concrete: training objectives are becoming shared language, with the pretrainfinetune recipe assembling them into the same two-stage workflow across modalities (Section 3); the Transformer, with emerging state-space alternatives in contention, is becoming shared encoder architecture (Section 4); and the representational object is shifting from parts to whole semantic units across every modality (Section 5). Part IIIThe Path to Unification (Sections 6 to 8) surveys the three-step progression toward omnimodal embeddings: transforming modalities into one another by rendering or serialization (Section 6), aligning independently encoded modalities (Section 7), and ultimately fusing them through deep interaction, in which joint embedding unifies and surpasses alignment (Section 8). To grade these paths we frame unification in terms of three progressively harder capabilities multimodal embedder must satisfycoverage, comparability, and compositionality, the 3C lenswhich we return to whenever single headline claim must be split into three questions: what the system takes in, what it can match, and what it can combine. Concretely, coverage asks which inputs the system has actually 7 Omnimodal Embeddings encoded and tested; comparability asks whether separately encoded inputs can be matched for specific task (e.g., whether text can retrieve relevant audio); and compositionality asks whether an output built from several inputs genuinely depends on all of them (e.g., whether an image and an edit instruction jointly define query). The three are progressively stronger, and the three paths satisfy them in turn: transformation broadens coverage, alignment enables comparability, and joint embedding aims at compositionality. Part IVThe Road Ahead (Sections 9 to 12) turns to what remains: the modality-specific properties true joint embedding must respect (Section 9), cross-pollination blueprint for reusing one modalitys methods in another (Section 10), the unified evaluation that we cannot yet build, organized around the 3C lens (Section 11), and closing outlook (Section 12). Per-modality cheat sheets are deferred to Appendix for readers who want quick history of single modality without interrupting the concept-first main thread. cross-modal previewdata objects, objectives, architectures, evaluation paradigms, and the exposed representational objectis given in Table 1, which highlights both the shared patterns and the modality-specific distinctions that motivate this work. To our knowledge, this paper is the first to provide unified treatment of embedding-model research across all major modalities from this cross-cutting, position-driven perspective.

sections.title: 2 A Unified Framework for Embedding Models
sections.content: Before tracing how the field is converging, we need shared vocabulary for what an embedding model isa static anatomy that applies to any modality, in any era. This section supplies that anatomy. We first decompose an embedding model into five recurring components and instantiate each across modalities (Section 2.1); we then sharpen the distinction between the input data unit and the output representational object (Section 2.2), which we argue is the key to understanding modality differences; and finally we introduce the analytical lensintersection, difference, and reusethat the rest of the paper uses to dissect the literature (Section 2.3). The framework here is deliberately static: it is taxonomy of the what. The companion Part II (Sections 3 to 5) is dynamic: it describes the howthe directions in which these components are moving. 2.1 The Anatomy of an Embedding Model Let denote data domain (e.g., the set of all English sentences, all RGB images, all audio waveforms, all graphs, all time series). An embedding model is parameterized function fθ : Rd (1) that maps each input to d-dimensional vector = fθ(x), referred to as an embedding or representation. The goal is for the geometry of the embedding space to reflect the semantic structure of the data: sim(ei, ej) semantic similarity(xi, xj), (2) where sim is similarity function, typically cosine similarity sim(u, v) = uv v or negative Euclidean distance dist(u, v) = v. When this map is well-learned, semantically similar inputs cluster together while dissimilar ones are pushed apart, enabling nearest-neighbor search, clustering, classification, and cross-modal alignment through simple vector operations. Beyond Euclidean and cosine metrics, alternatives include geodesic distances in hyperbolic geometries that embed hierarchies with low distortion for knowledge taxonomies, graphs, and images (Nickel & Kiela, 2017; Lin et al., 2023c; Khrulkov et al., 2020), and dynamic time warping (DTW), the long-standing native measure for time series (Sakoe & Chiba, 1978). Whatever the modality, almost every modern embedding model can be decomposed into five components. The components are defined by their role, not by any particular implementation, which 8 Omnimodal Embeddings Table 1: The anatomy of an embedding model. The intended use should determine what is embedded, how inputs interact, how outputs are pooled, and which information must be retained. Structural components (data unit, tokenizer, encoder, aggregation, representational object) are distinguished from the modeling decisions (objective, evaluation). is what makes the decomposition modality-agnostic. Table 1 summarizes them, and Figure 2 shows the role each part plays in the life cycle of an embedding model. (1) Data unit and tokenization. Raw data must be carved into units and mapped to tokens before any encoder can act. What counts as unit is modeling choice: for text it is subword piece (Bojanowski et al., 2017), sentence, or document; for image pixel, patch (Dosovitskiy et al., 2021), or region; for audio waveform sample, spectrogram frame, continuous latent frame (Baevski et al., 2020), or codec token (Défossez et al., 2023); for graph node, an edge, subgraph, or typed triple (Khoshraftar & An, 2024); for time series timestamp, window, or patch (Nie et al., 2023); for table cell, header, row, or column (Deng et al., 2020; Iida et al., 2021). Here token denotes units role in sequence rather than membership in finite discrete vocabulary (detailed in Section 5.1). (2) Encoder architecture. The encoder turns sequence (or set) of tokens into sequence of hidden states. While the families differCNNs for vision, GNNs for graphs, RNNs and TCNs for time series, Transformers everywherethe field is converging on the Transformer as the default backbone (see Section 4). Modality-specific architectures (CNNs, GNNs, RNNs) are best understood not as alternatives to the Transformer but as encodings of strong domain priors that the Transformer omits: translation equivariance for CNNs, permutation equivariance over prescribed topology for GNNs, temporal recurrence for RNNs (Bronstein et al., 2021). (3) Aggregation and representational object. The encoder emits sequence of hidden states (h1, . . . , hL); what is read out from themthe representational object that downstream consumers actually useis second modeling choice, distinct from the input-side choice of data unit. Common 9 Omnimodal Embeddings Table 2: Different representational objects support different uses and entail different trade-offs. The representational object is exposed to downstream consumers; this choicenot the encoderdecides what an embedding can do. Output format Form Typical uses Main trade-off Global dense vector Local vector sequence/set Rd RNd Discrete codes {1, . . . , K}L Probability distribution p(z x) ANN retrieval, clustering, linear probes Grounding, late interaction, reranking Compression, generation, sequence modeling Ambiguity, calibration, risk-aware retrieval Magnitudepreserving vector Rd (scale retained) Time-series retrieval where amplitude is the semantics Loss of fine spatial, temporal and relational evidence Larger indexes and less predictable storage Quantization loss and potentially unstable code semantics More complex indexing than point vectors Must balance scale sensitivity against the shape invariance that aids cross-domain transfer aggregation strategies include the [CLS] token of BERT-style models, mean pooling, attention-based pooling (Lee et al., 2025a), and the last tokens representation for LLM-based embedders. Crossmodal variation here is instructive: audio speaker models use statistics pooling (mean and standard deviation across frames), deliberately keeping the second moments that text-side global pooling would erase (Snyder et al., 2018); dense vision models instead keep the set of patch vectors for lateinteraction retrieval (Faysse et al., 2025). The recurring insight is that the granularity of the resulting object trades off expressiveness against comparability: single global vector is computationally efficient to index and compare but discards location, multiplicity, and correspondence, whereas sequence of local vectors preserves them at storage and comparison costa tension we revisit in Section 2.2. (4) Training objective. The loss shapes the geometry. Four families recur across modalities: contrastive objectives pull positives together and push negatives apart; reconstructive objectives mask part of the input and predict it back; generative objectives train decoder (autoencoder, VAE, GAN, or diffusion) and reuse its latent; and hybrid objectivesof which UniLM (Dong et al., 2019) and GRIT (Muennighoff et al., 2025) are the emblemsjointly optimize for representation and generation. Section 3 argues that the contrastive paradigm has become the lingua franca across modalities, even where pretraining is reconstructive. (5) Evaluation paradigm. Embedding quality is measured by freezing the encoder and probing it on diverse suite of downstream tasks. Text standardized it in SentEvals frozen-representation probes (Conneau & Kiela, 2018), audio adopted it with SUPERB (Yang et al., 2021), and MTEB scaled it into massive text suite (Muennighoff et al., 2023). What varies is the task family: retrieval and semantic textual similarity for text, classification and detection for vision, recognition and tagging for audio, node classification and link prediction for graphs, forecasting and anomaly detection for time series. The fragmentation of these benchmarkseach modality developing its own MXEB (MTEB for text, MIEB for image, MAEB for audio)is itself symptom of the silos we document in Section 1 and confront in Section 11. The point of this anatomy is that the five components are orthogonal axes: one can swap the encoder while holding the objective fixed, or change the representational object while holding the encoder fixed. Cross-modal convergence, the theme of Part II, is largely the observation that on four of these five axes the same choices are increasingly being made in every modality. 2.2 Data and Representational Objects subtle but pervasive confusion in the literature conflates the model input (the data unit) with the extracted output (the representational object). The data unit is the atom of the input; the representational object is the atom of the outputthe object that carries semantics and that downstream 10 Omnimodal Embeddings consumers actually use. Distinguishing the two is essential because the choice of representational object decides what an embedding can do. Concretely, the same encoder can expose any of five distinct objects  (Table 2)  : single global vector Rd for compact indexing; sequence or set of local vectors RNd for dense prediction and late interaction (Faysse et al., 2025); sequence of discrete codes {1, . . . , K}L that bridges continuous signals to the language-model interface (van den Oord et al., 2017; Hsu et al., 2021; Défossez et al., 2023); probability distribution p(z x) that captures ambiguity (Kingma & Welling, 2014; Chun et al., 2021); or magnitude-preserving vector that retains numerical scale (Lin et al., 2024). We unpack the trade-offs among these five readouts in Section 5.1. Each readout reflects commitment to which information must survive the interface and which may be discarded. This choice underpins the difference analysis of Section 9, while Section 5 develops its dynamic complementthe granularity shift, in which the preferred object is moving up from parts toward whole semantic units in every modality. 2.3 Our Analytical Lens: Intersection, Difference, and Reuse To reason across modalities without collapsing their distinctions, we adopt three-part lens, applied uniformly in every subsequent chapter. Intersectionthe shared core: the mathematical principles, architectures, and paradigms that recur across modalities. The InfoNCE loss, the Transformer, the pretrainfinetune recipe, and the frozen-encoder evaluation protocol are intersections. Part II is, in effect, catalog of intersections. Differencethe modality-specific core: the challenges, data properties, and methods that belong to one modality because they derive from the structure of its inputs. Audios superposition of factors, graphs explicit relational structure, time series continuous axis and non-standardized units are differences. Section 9 enumerates them. Reusethe directional transfer: how methodology born in one modality is borrowed and adapted by another. Contrastive learning moving from vision to text to audio represents reuse. The cross-pollination map of Section 10 is deliberate exercise in planning reuse. These three categories are not partitiona single finding often sits on the boundary. Audios superposition of factors is difference, but the disentanglement methods it provoked are candidate reuse target for other modalities; the Transformer is an intersection, yet the question of which positional encoding to inject is difference. The lens is what keeps the comparison honest: it lets us state, for each technique, not merely that it exists but which modality owns the problem and which is borrowing the solution. Static anatomy, dynamic evolution. The framework above is static anatomy: taxonomy that tells us what an embedding model is made of, usable in any era and any modality. It defines our nouns: encoder, objective, and representational object, which supplies the coordinate system in which the rest of the paper plots the trajectory of the field. Part II is dynamic evolution: it describes what is changing within the slots this taxonomy provides. It defines our verbs: the Transformer is becoming the universal encoder, contrastive learning is becoming the lingua franca, the pretrainfinetune recipe is standardizing the training workflow, and the field is shifting its favored representational object upward, from tokens and pixels to sentences and imageseach sense in which the separate modality literatures are converging toward one another. Finally, because convergence spans several independent design choices, Figure 3 separates four distinct meanings: architecture reuse, objective reuse, coordinate alignment, and parameter sharing. shared trunk does not entail aligned retrieval vectors (as in Meta-Transformer; Zhang et al., 2023c), nor vice versa (as in ImageBind; Girdhar et al., 2023), while systems such as OneLLM (Han et al., 2024) and VLM2Vec (Jiang et al., 2025) combine both. 11 Omnimodal Embeddings Figure 3: Four meanings of convergence shown separately for illustrative systems. system can align outputs from modality-specific encoders without sharing their encoder weights (IMAGEBIND), or reuse encoder parameters without creating one aligned retrieval space (META-TRANSFORMER). Qualified marks partial architectural reuse or interfaces whose status depends on the component examined. 12 Omnimodal Embeddings

sections.title: 3 Training Objectives: The Lingua Franca
sections.content: If there is single force driving the convergence documented in Section 1, it is the convergence of training objectives. Across modalities, the same handful of lossescontrastive, reconstructive, and increasingly generativehybridnow account for the overwhelming majority of state-of-the-art embedding models. This chapter examines each family through our intersection/difference lens: in every case the mechanism (the loss) is an intersection shared across modalities, while the construction of the prediction targetwhat is pulled together, what is masked, what is reconstructedis difference that reflects the structure of each modalitys data. The convergence, moreover, is not only in the losses but in the workflow that stages them: pretrain first, finetune second is now the common recipe in every modality. 3.1 Contrastive Objectives The contrastive paradigm is the dominant force in modern embedding research. Its core is simple: given an anchor x, attract positive x+ (a semantically equivalent or related sample) and repel negatives (unrelated samples) in the embedding space. The shared mechanism. The most widely used instantiation is the InfoNCE loss (van den Oord et al., 2018): LInfoNCE = log exp(cid:0)sim(e, e+)/τ(cid:1) j=1 exp(cid:0)sim(e, ej)/τ(cid:1) , (3) where = fθ(x), e+ = fθ(x+), τ is temperature, and the denominator sums one positive with N1 negatives (often in-batch). InfoNCE is categorical cross-entropy in which the positive is the correct class among candidates; under standard positiveand negative-sampling assumptions, log LInfoNCE lower-bounds the mutual information between views of the input (van den Oord et al., 2018; Wu et al., 2018). Its normalized variant, NT-Xent (Chen et al., 2020b), projects embeddings to the unit hypersphere before scoring to encourage uniformity, while the earlier triplet loss (Schroff et al., 2015) directly enforces margin between the positive and negative distances. These forms are modality-agnostic: the loss does not know whether the input comes from an image, sentence, or graph. What differs across modalities is entirely in how the positive x+ and negatives are constructed, which is where each modalitys structure enters. Difference: how each modality builds its pairs. Contrastive learning is machine for encoding chosen invariance (Chen et al., 2020b), and the augmentation set declares what transformations should leave the semantics unchanged. The modalities differ in how easy that declaration is. Textfrom discrete edits to implicit augmentation. Text has no natural geometric augmentation, so its positives were initially manufactured by discrete edits: EDA composes synonym replacement, random insertion, swap, and deletion (Wei & Zou, 2019); AEDA reduces this to random insertion of punctuation marks (Karimi et al., 2021); UDA builds consistency objective out of such augmented views (Xie et al., 2020); and TMix interpolates the hidden states of two sentences, moving the augmentation into the encoders latent space (Chen et al., 2020a). SimCSE (Gao et al., 2021) then made the augmentation entirely implicit: the same sentence passes the encoder twice, and the stochasticity of independent dropout masks in the encoder produces two slightly different embeddings of the same inputan elegant, data-free positive sampling method. 13 Omnimodal Embeddings Table 3: The contrastive objective is shared across modalities, but the choice of positive pair defines what the embedding should treat as unchangedthe declared invariance. The mechanism (InfoNCE) is an intersection; the positive construction and its characteristic failure are the difference. Modality Typical positive Intended invariant Characteristic failure Text Vision Audio Graph views, paraqueryrelevant Dropout phrase, passage Crops views of one image or photometric Surface variation under semantic equivalence Viewpoint and appearance change Two utterance views or an audiocaption pair Content, speaker, event, or scene, depending on task Augmented views, nearby nodes, valid triples Topological proximity or relation compatibility Time series Windows, scales, or time frequency views Shape, regime, or instance identity Cross-modal Co-observed or captioned objects Shared semantic content False negatives and lexical shortcuts (Gao et al., 2021; Xiong et al., 2021) Cropping removes the discriminating object (He et al., 2020) desired factor for one task is nuisance for another (Elizalde et al., 2023) Node/edge dropout changes graph semantics (You et al., 2020; Wei et al., 2023) Jitter, scaling and warping are domain-dependent (Yue et al., 2022) Co-occurrence is partial or asynchronous (Radford et al., 2021; Girdhar et al., 2023) Visionthe paradigms birthplace. Contrastive learning originated and matured in vision, spanning from the Siamese network of signature verification (Bromley et al., 1993) to the modern instantiations. Random crops, color jitter, and flips preserve the semantic identity of an object (Chen et al., 2020b), with MoCos momentum encoder maintaining large, consistent negative queue (He et al., 2020), while the negative-free branches replace repulsion with bootstrapping (Grill et al., 2020; Chen & He, 2021) or redundancy reduction (Zbontar et al., 2021). The familys maturity has landmark: self-supervised pretraining in vision now matches or beats supervised training on standard benchmarks (Caron et al., 2021; He et al., 2022)the outcome that made this recipe the template the other modalities would follow. Visionlanguagenaturally paired data. Where single modalities must manufacture positives, the web naturally provides abundant paired data for visionlanguage: caption and its image are positive by construction (Radford et al., 2021). Audiofrom waveform corruption to quantized targets and language pairing. Analogous to visions crop-and-jitter family, audio manufactured positives by waveform-level augmentations: pitch shifting and time stretching, additive noise injected at controlled SNR, and reverberation via convolution with measured or simulated room impulse responses (Ko et al., 2015; Salamon & Bello, 2017; Allen & Berkley, 1979). The newer constructions are less hand-crafted: wav2vec 2.0 masks latent frames and contrasts them against quantized targets derived from the same audio (Baevski et al., 2020); CLAP ports the CLIP recipe to (audio, caption) pairs (Elizalde et al., 2023), with successors manufacturing the semantic spread that closed-vocabulary tag captions lack (Wu et al., 2023b; Dinkel et al., 2025; Takano et al., 2025). Codeviews as positives. Code can have many different forms that describe the same behavior. Its positive includes semantically equivalent view of the same program: its docstring, abstract syntax tree (AST), data-flow graph, or semantics-preserving refactor (Wang et al., 2021a; Li et al., 2022b; Wang et al., 2022c; Guo et al., 2022), which is what turns contrastive learning into probe of executable semantics rather than surface form. Graphview construction over structure. Graph contrastive methods define positive and negative graphs through structural augmentations such as node/edge dropout and feature masking; the contrastive and generative families are distinguished by the operation that creates the learning signal (You et al., 2020; Wei et al., 2023; Jin et al., 2023b; Chen et al., 2024c). Time seriesthe augmentation problem. Here the construction is hardest: jittering, scaling, permutation, and warping each encode an invariance that holds in some domains and 14 Omnimodal Embeddings fails in othersaugmentations that are beneficial elsewhere can actively hurt here (Yue et al., 2022), which is why TF-C pools bank of augmentations rather than trusting any single transform (Zhang et al., 2022b). Time series confronts most starkly the truth that an augmentation is declared invariance; the principled responses either declare the invariance architecturally (Gao et al., 2023a; Germain et al., 2025) or contrast across time-frequency views (Zhang et al., 2022b; Fraikin et al., 2024) and multi-rate sampling hierarchies (Duan et al., 2024). The recurring insight is that the InfoNCE mechanism is constant; what each modality supplies is its knowledge of which transformations are meaning-preserving. Texts dropout trick and time series declared-symmetry convolutions are the same idea arrived at from opposite ends of the augmentation spectrum: manufacture positive by stating an invariance. Table 3 makes the mechanismversus-difference split explicit: the same equation means different things in each modality because the positive pair declares different invariance, and the recurring failure is the augmentation that abuses it. Hard negatives and the alignmentuniformity decomposition. Two further shared refinements recur across modalities. Random in-batch negatives are often too easy; hard negative miningselecting negatives close to the anchor but semantically distinctis critical for dense retrieval (Karpukhin et al., 2020; Xiong et al., 2021) and reappears as batch construction in modern LLM embedders (Lee et al., 2025a; Zhang et al., 2026b). And for the standard normalized contrastive loss, the asymptotic analysis of Wang & Isola (2020) motivates two measurable quantitiesthe expected closeness of positives (alignment) and the spread of normalized embeddings on the hypersphere (uniformity)which give modality-agnostic design lens and diagnostic used from text (Gao et al., 2021) to time series (Jalali et al., 2025). Negative-free contrastive learning. The same decomposition suggests that repulsion admits substitute: what negatives prevent is collapse, and the negative-free branches of the vision lineage show two ways to prevent it without negatives. The first is architectural bootstrapping: BYOL learns by predicting an exponential-moving-average copy of itself (Grill et al., 2020), and SimSiam reduces this to plain Siamese pair whose predictor-and-stop-gradient asymmetry alone prevents collapse (Chen & He, 2021). The second is redundancy reduction: the learning signal lives in the statistics of the embedding batch rather than in pairwise comparisons. SwAV enforces consistency of cluster assignments across views, spreading the batch against learned prototypes (Caron et al., 2020); Barlow Twins drives the cross-correlation matrix of the two views embeddings toward the identity (Zbontar et al., 2021), so each embedding dimension is stable across views yet nonredundant with the others; VICReg states the same goal as explicit variance, invariance, and covariance terms (Bardes et al., 2022), with the variance floor alone preventing collapse. Both routes keep the objective negative-free while still filling the uniformity half of the decomposition: the former places the anti-collapse pressure in an architectural asymmetry, the latter in the batchs own moments. 3.2 Reconstructive Objectives While contrastive learning operates on relative relationships, reconstructive objectives learn representations by recovering masked or corrupted portions of the input. The shared mechanism is mask and predict; the difference is what is masked and what constitutes correct prediction. The shared mechanism. representative reconstructive loss masks set of positions and trains the model to predict the masked content from the remainder xM: Lrec = EM (cid:35) ℓ( ˆxi, xi) , (cid:34) iM 15 (4) Omnimodal Embeddings where ℓ is typically cross-entropy for discrete targets and MSE for continuous targets. The encoder, forced to summarize enough of the input to fill in the gaps, learns rich contextual representations that are then finetuned with contrastive or supervised objectives for downstream embedding tasks. Difference: what is masked and predicted. Textdiscrete token IDs. BERT (Devlin et al., 2019) masks tokens and predicts discrete token ID from finite vocabularya semantically loaded discrete symbol. Codestructure-aware targets. Code inherited MLM from BERT but quickly made the target richer than token IDs: CodeBERT (Feng et al., 2020) adds replaced-token detection over (NL, code) pairs, GraphCodeBERT (Guo et al., 2021) predicts data-flow edges, and CodeT5 (Wang et al., 2021b) masks identifiers so the model must infer what an obfuscated variable does. The masked target thus encodes ever deeper structure: surface token syntax semantics. Visionhigh-ratio continuous pixels. MAE (He et al., 2022) masks large fraction (75%) of image patches and reconstructs the raw continuous pixels; the asymmetry between deep encoder on visible patches and shallow decoder for all forces the encoder to capture semantics. Audiocluster IDs, spectrogram patches, and learned targets. HuBERT (Hsu et al., 2021) masks latent features and predicts offline cluster assignments, refined across rounds; AudioMAE (Huang et al., 2022a) masks spectrogram patches and regresses toward the raw spectrogram; data2vec instead regresses toward contextualized representations built by an exponentialmoving-average teacher (Baevski et al., 2022); and BEATs predicts discrete labels generated by learned acoustic tokenizer (Chen et al., 2023c). Graphhidden structure and attributes. Graph reconstructive methods reconstruct hidden structure or attributes: masked edges (Li et al., 2023c), or node features (Hou et al., 2022) from partially observed graphs. KG completion methods score entityrelation triples against corrupted candidates (Bordes et al., 2013; Sun et al., 2019). Tablecells, entities, and structure. Among table encoders, TURL recovers the entity behind masked cell (Deng et al., 2020), TABBIE detects corrupted cell among intact ones (Iida et al., 2021), and table-based QA models such as TaPas/TaBERT recover table-conditioned text (Herzig et al., 2020; Yin et al., 2020). The masked target is thus neither token ID nor pixel but typed cell contenta unit whose meaning comes jointly from its value, its header, and its rowcolumn position. Time seriesthe interpolation pitfall. Masked patch reconstruction is the continuous analogue of MLM, but where the language version predicts semantically loaded symbol, the continuous version regresses toward conditional mean that is dominated by interpolation for smooth signal, so recovering trend and seasonality is the expected outcome, not failure of capacity (Nie et al., 2023; Wilinski et al., 2025). This difference explains why reconstruction works cleanly for modalities with predefined semantic units and weakly for continuous series without them. The contrast is revealing: reconstructive pretraining gives strong initialization when the masked target carries meaning independent of its context, such as discrete tokens, discrete cluster IDs, and object pixels. Where the target is smooth interpolation of its neighbors, as in much of time series, the learned representation encodes low-order structure that classical decomposition already extracted without learning. 3.3 Generative and Hybrid Objectives third family learns representations as byproduct of generating the data, and recent, increasingly important trend unifies generative and representational objectives. Generative objectives for representation. The generative label fixes what must be predicted during training, whereas the form of the exposed representation remains separate design choice just as MAE trains under generative pretext loss yet yields transferable continuous encoder (He 16 Omnimodal Embeddings et al., 2022), generative models can expose latents that are distributional, continuous, or discrete. Variational autoencoders (Kingma & Welling, 2014) expose distributional latent p(z x) that captures multiplicity and uncertainty, which is useful when an input corresponds to several semantic readings, as an image matches many captions (Chun et al., 2021). GAN-based encoders (Donahue et al., 2017; Song et al., 2018) learn data-to-latent mapping that inverts the generator, and its output doubles as an embedding. Diffusion models contribute latents too: latent diffusion generates in compressed autoencoder space (Rombach et al., 2022), diffusion autoencoders factor semantic code from stochastic detail (Preechakul et al., 2022), and DIFT shows that intermediate diffusion features yield strong zero-shot correspondence (Tang et al., 2023). parallel line vector-quantizes continuous features into discrete codebook indices that autoregressive models can consumeVQVAE in vision (van den Oord et al., 2017), and neural codecs in audio (Zeghidour et al., 2022; Défossez et al., 2023), whose semantic/acoustic token split now organizes the speech-language stack, whether the semantics are distilled into the codecs own codebooks (Zhang et al., 2023b) or quantized by codec learned over pretrained speech representations (Huang et al., 2024b). Hybrid: the unification of representation and generation. This unification began in the text world when UniLM jointly optimized bidirectional, unidirectional, and sequence-to-sequence language modeling objectives within single Transformer via varying attention masks (Dong et al., 2019). Shortly after, T5 unified representation and generation tasks by casting them both into sequence-to-sequence modeling format (Raffel et al., 2020), and Unified-IO extended it into the multimodal setting, committing text, images, and structured outputs to one shared discrete-token vocabulary (Lu et al., 2023a; 2024). In the LLM era, GRIT (Muennighoff et al., 2025) represents an early signal of convergence between representation and generation, jointly training single LLM with contrastive loss for embedding and an autoregressive loss for generation, using instruction prefixes to disambiguate the tasks. The unification is spreading: latent diffusion transfers selfsupervised geometry into diffusion-transformer states (Yu et al., 2025), MergeVQ jointly optimizes representation and generation with token merging and quantization (Li et al., 2025d), and earlyfusion models interleave text and visual tokens in single autoregressive stream (Team, 2024). Audiolanguage models add scaling law of their own: continual generative pretraining before contrastive training raises the ceiling on representation quality (Xiao et al., 2025a; Yoo et al., 2026). The unification also runs in reverse, where pretrained encoders extend LLMs rather than fuse into them: E2LLM feeds an LLM soft prompts compressed from long contexts by text encoder (Liao et al., 2025), and GALLa aligns GNNs structural embeddings into code LLM as an auxiliary training objective (Zhang et al., 2025f). What is emerging is view in which representation and generation are not opposed but two heads of the same objectivea unification that the joint embedding models of Section 8 will push to its logical conclusion. Knowledge distillation. practical hybrid across all modalities is distillation, in which compact student mimics powerful teachers embedding space. Self-distillation underlies DINO in vision, where the teacher is an exponential moving average of the student (Caron et al., 2021), and increasingly text, where BGE-M3 distills from teacher signal built as the weighted integration of its dense, sparse, and multi-vector relevance scores (Chen et al., 2024b); cross-encoder-to-bi-encoder distillation is standard in training dense retrievers (Ren et al., 2021), and extends into the LLM regime (Liao et al., 2024). Where strong teacher exists, distillation is the most economic route to modality-agnostic embedding, and it is the mechanism behind many modern multimodal embedders (Gu et al., 2025). 3.4 The PretrainFinetune Recipe The three loss families above, for all their differences, are rarely applied standalone: across modalities they are assembled into common pipeline. The dominant recipe is to pretrain on large-scale unlabeled or weakly-supervised data, then finetune on task-specific or contrastive data. This recipe is integral to the discussion of training objectives, and like them it is an intersection, whose differences lie only in how the stages are filled. 17 Omnimodal Embeddings Intersection: one recipe, every modality. The two-stage framework recurs everywhere. In text, BERT pretrains with MLM and then finetunes on downstream tasks (Devlin et al., 2019); SimCSE shows the second stage can itself be contrastive and unlabeled, adapting pretrained encoder with dropout-induced positives (Gao et al., 2021); and E5 shows the first stage can be contrastive too, mining weakly-supervised pairs from the web and relying on supervised finetuning for the strongest results (Wang et al., 2022a). In vision, MAE and DINO pretrain by reconstruction and self-distillation, respectively, and transfer by finetuning or linear probing (Caron et al., 2021; He et al., 2022). In audio, wav2vec 2.0 pretrains on unlabeled speech and then finetunes on as little as ten minutes of transcribed speech (Baevski et al., 2020). In graphs, pretraining must cover both grains of the data at once: combining node-level and graph-level pretraining avoids the negative transfer that either alone can cause (Hu et al., 2020b; Kong et al., 2025). In tables, TaBERT and TaPas pretrain on tables and accompanying text and then finetune on downstream tasks such as table question answering (Yin et al., 2020; Herzig et al., 2020). The recipe even survives the shift from encoders to LLM embedders, where stage one is typically generative pretraining and stage two contrastive, instruction-conditioned finetuning (Su et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024d; Lee et al., 2025a); audiolanguage embedders document the same swap of objectives into the same slots, with generative stage one raising the ceiling of the contrastive stage two (Section 3.3). What persists across all of these is not any particular loss but the staging: accessible universal signal first, expensive task-specific signal second. Difference: what fills each stage. What the modality determines is what counts as pretraining materialraw text, unlabeled speech, web imagecaption pairs, contrastively mined sentence pairsand what the finetuning signal is: labels, pairs, or instructions. The boundary cases show the recipe is considered choice rather than law. CLIP-style models collapse the pipeline: where the web-scale paired data is readily available, the contrastive stage becomes the pretraining, and zero-shot transfer replaces finetuning (Radford et al., 2021). And the graph case above warns that the pipeline can even hurt when its first stage is mismatched to the modalitys structure, restating this chapters mechanism-versus-difference split at the level of the workflow. Takeaway The core takeaway of this chapter is convergence-with-difference. The InfoNCE loss, the mask-and-predict recipe, the representationgeneration unification, and the pretrainfinetune workflow are intersectionsthe same machinery running in every modality. What differs is the raw material each modality gives that machinery: dropout-induced positive for text, cropped view for vision, quantized target for audio, structural augmentation for graphs, and declared symmetry for time series. The objective is the lingua franca; the data unit decides what can be said in it.

sections.title: 4 Architectures: The Universal Encoder
sections.content: The second axis of convergence is architectural: the Transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017) is becoming the default encoder across modalitiesViT for images (Dosovitskiy et al., 2021), audio Transformers for speech (Baevski et al., 2020), Graph Transformers for structured data (Geisler et al., 2023), patch Transformers for time series (Nie et al., 2023), and decoder-only LLMs for text (Wang et al., 2024d; Lee et al., 2025a). This chapter explains why single architecture can serve as universal backbone across all modalities, and, equally important, when modality-specific architecture still remains justified. We also weigh the most prominent challenger to the Transformers ubiquitystate space models and their linear-attention relativeswhich by now spans nearly every modality itself, and ask what the contest turns on for embedding models specifically. 18 Omnimodal Embeddings 4.1 The Transformer as Universal Backbone We argue the Transformer converges as universal encoder because four interlocking properties make it the most flexible architecture that remains practically trainable at scale. Weak inductive bias: self-attention as set operator. The Geometric Deep Learning framework (Bronstein et al., 2021) unifies architectures by the symmetry assumptions they encode: CNNs assume translation equivariance and locality; RNNs assume temporal equivariance and Markovian structure; GNNs assume permutation equivariance over prescribed graph topology. The Transformers core mechanism assumes none of these: self-attention is permutation-equivariant set operation. Each token issues query, compares it against all keys, and receives weighted sum of all values; the operation treats its input as an unordered token set in which every element may interact with every other, and it presumes no particular spatial or temporal structureneither the locality of CNNs nor the sequentiality of RNNs. Concretely, absent positional encodings and causal masks, permuting the input tokens permutes the token-level outputs in step (Yun et al., 2020), and pooled readout such as [CLS] or mean pooling then aggregates the equivariant token outputs into permutation-invariant embedding. From the GNN perspective, self-attention is message-passing on complete graph with learned edge weights, rather than topology prescribed by domain structure (Bronstein et al., 2021; Mijangos et al., 2025). By the criteria of Battaglia et al. (2018), this all-to-all interaction carries correspondingly weak relational inductive bias: it makes no assumption about which elements should interact, only that any interaction is possible. The trade-off is data tax: strong priors enable fast convergence in low-data regimes but constrain the solution space, whereas the Transformers weak bias requires more data but can learn representations less constrained by hand-designed priors (Dosovitskiy et al., 2021). Empirically, under matched training, Transformers exhibit stronger out-of-distribution generalization than CNNs (Bai et al., 2021), and ViT representations are markedly more uniform across layers than CNNs, because self-attention enables early global information aggregation (Raghu et al., 2021). And the mechanism is expressive enough to be universal approximator of continuous permutation-equivariant sequence-to-sequence functions (Yun et al., 2020), with even two-layer attention-only architectures sufficing (Hu et al., 2025a), while cross-attention extends it to universal bipartite relational operator for multimodal fusion (Section 8). This is why it is universal: any modality that can be tokenized into set can be processed by Transformer. Tokenization: the modality interface. Tokenizationconverting raw data into sequence of discrete or continuous tokensis the abstraction that makes the Transformer modality-agnostic: subword units for text, patches for images (Dosovitskiy et al., 2021), spectrogram patches for audio, continuous waveform features for speech (Baevski et al., 2020), codec tokens for codec-based speech models, node features for graphs, time-window segments for time series (Nie et al., 2023), and cells for tables (Herzig et al., 2020; Iida et al., 2021). Meta-Transformer (Zhang et al., 2023c) demonstrates this explicitly: the same frozen encoder, with modality-specific tokenizers and lightweight heads, processes 12 modalities without any paired cross-modal data. data2vec (Baevski et al., 2022) pushes the point further: one self-supervised reconstruction objective serves speech, vision, and language alike, with only the input processing, masking scheme, and target normalization adapting to each modality. Figure 4 shows the resulting picture: modality-specific tokenizer is the prerequisite for interfacing with the shared processing core, and Table 4 records what the tokenizer emits for each named modality and which symmetry its index structure carries (e.g., translation equivariance over regular lattice or permutation invariance over an unordered set). This structure decides how the missing prior should be re-injected: through positional encoding over the lattice indices, or through features supplied by the tokenizer or attention bias. Adding structure back: positional encoding as plug-in prior. At first glance, the same orderagnosticism that makes the Transformer universal is defect for modalities in which order matters: text is sequential, time series is ordered in time, graphs edges carry fixed relations. The resolution is architectural: for any modality where order is meaningful, positional encodings explicitly reintroduce the structural prior. Text and time series use absolute or relative positional encodings over their 19 Omnimodal Embeddings Text / Code subwords + order Image / Video patches/tubelets + t, x, Audio Graph frames/codes + rate nodes/edges + topology Time Series windows + time/var ID Shared processing core Transformer / SSM / Experts global metric vector local / structured vectors input-specific info + uncertainty Figure 4: shared processing core with modality-specific tokenizers and external structural information. Self-attention is permutation-equivariant and order-agnostic, while state space models impose strictly one-dimensional scan. In either case, order, topology, rate, and variable identity must be re-supplied through positional encodings, scan orders, attention biases, edge features, or timestamped tokens. indices; graphs inject structural encodings, attention biases, or edge features that expose topology to the otherwise structure-free attention (Tao et al., 2025; Yuan et al., 2026); audio may attach timestamps to codec tokens; and table encoders keep the 2D grid by attaching explicit row and column index embeddings to each token (Herzig et al., 2020), or applying vertical self-attention across the rows aligned to given column (Yin et al., 2020). This core mechanism plus pluggable priors design is the source of the Transformers flexibility: one operator with weak spatial and temporal priors, combined with modality-specific positional scheme, spans the whole range from unordered graphs to strictly ordered time series. In Battaglia et al. (2018)s terms, the weak relational bias is the base layer on which modality priors are stacked as needed. Scalability and parallelizability. Unlike RNNs, Transformers process all tokens in parallel after computing attention scores, making training on hundreds of billions of tokens feasible in wall-clock time; and unlike MLPs (Bengio et al., 2000)which likewise impose weak structural priorsthey exchange information across tokens with parameter count independent of context length. Scaling laws (Kaplan et al., 2020; Hoffmann et al., 2022) give predictable improvement as function of size, data, and compute, and the Transformer is uniquely amenable to exploiting these laws at scale. Platonic-representation evidence (Huh et al., 2024) that larger models across modalities grow increasingly aligned comports with the idea that the Transformers architectural generality both enables and accelerates the convergence. These four properties, taken together, reach their natural limit in one further arrangement: single shared trunk, front-ended by modality-specific tokenizers and lightweight heads, serving every modality at once. The feasibility of such modality-agnostic processing was first sketched by MultiModels shared body over image, speech, and text (Kaiser et al., 2017) and most prominently established by Perceiver and its successors (Jaegle et al., 2021; 2022; Zhu et al., 2022; Li et al., 2023a), which showed that one Transformer can process inputs as diverse as images, audio, and point clouds with minimal modality-specific assumptions. We name this arrangement the shared backbone. It is instantiated later by Meta-Transformer across twelve modalities (Zhang et al., 2023c), 4M-21 across twenty-one (Bachmann et al., 2024), and OneLLM binding additional modalities into one languagecentered trunk through universal projection module (Han et al., 2024). We keep it conceptually separate from the three bridges of Part III because what it shares is parameters, not representations: sharing parameters alone leaves the per-modality outputs tied by no learned cross-modal metric, and cross-modal retrieval requires at least an alignment objective on top of the trunkadded, for instance, by Uni-Perceivers shared cosine-similarity loss (Zhu et al., 2022). The shared backbone is 20 Omnimodal Embeddings Table 4: The tokenizer, rather than the Transformer trunk, is where named modalities remain distinct. We group modalities by the symmetry their index structure carries. Translation-symmetry modalities are indexed by regular lattice (image, video, spectrogram, time index), so each token has fixed address that positional encoding can name directly; Permutation-symmetry modalities (point cloud, table, graph) live on an unordered set with no natural lattice; here self-attentions own permutation equivariance matches the domain, but relational structure must be supplied through the tokenizer or attention bias. Yin et al., 2020) Node-feature tokens plus learned centrality, shortest-path and edge encodings (Khoshraftar & An, 2024) Local point-group token Permutation invariance over metric set One token per categorical/numerical field Permutation invariance over keyed fields Node token with structural attention biases Permutation equivariance over relational set therefore best read not as route toward unifying representations but as the culminating evidence of the architectural convergence chronicled in this Part. 4.2 The Rival Universal Encoder: State Space Models and Linear Attention Before accepting the Transformer as the universal encoder, we must first examine its most prominent rivaland the rivals own trajectory turns out to confirm, rather than contradict, the convergence this Part documents. second family born cross-modal. The structured state space line begins with S4, proposed explicitly as step toward general-purpose sequence model and evaluated at birth on text, image, speech, and time series (Gu et al., 2022); it is streamlined by S5 (Smith et al., 2023) and culminates in Mamba, whose selective SSM (named S6) lets the recurrences parameters depend on the input, so that the model chooses token by token what its fixed-size state keepswith stateof-the-art results reported across language, audio, and genomics (Gu & Dao, 2023). The family 21 Omnimodal Embeddings has since swept the modalities at speed rivaling the Transformers own: Vim and VMamba for images (Zhu et al., 2024b; Liu et al., 2024c), Audio Mamba for spectrograms (Erol et al., 2024), S-Mamba for time-series (Wang et al., 2025d), Graph Mamba for graphs (Behrouz & Hashemi, 2024), and long-range DNA sequence modelsspanning implicit-convolutional relatives such as HyenaDNA and bidirectional Mamba backbones such as Caduceuswith context lengths up to million nucleotides (Nguyen et al., 2023; Schiff et al., 2024). And the sweep reuses the recipe of Section 4.1 rather than replacing it: SSMs consume the same tokenization interface (Vim simply takes ViT patches), and the structure that attention recovers through positional encodings must be re-injected through the same pluggable priorsposition embeddings plus bidirectional scans for Vims image sequences, cross-scan traversing the spatial axes for VMamba, neighborhood tokenization and explicit token ordering for Graph Mamba (Zhu et al., 2024b; Liu et al., 2024c; Behrouz & Hashemi, 2024). Even here, modality differences reassert themselves. Mambas own ablations find input-dependent selection (the S4-to-S6 change) decisive for discrete, informationdense sequences like language, while on continuous, smoothly varying signals such as raw audio waveforms the non-selective LTI recurrence (S4) remains preferable, its time-invariance matching the signals structure (Gu & Dao, 2023). This reinforces the core lesson of this Part: the mechanism is the intersection, and the data decides. What the fixed state yields, and what it sacrifices. Where attention keeps every token available to every other, an SSM compresses the past into fixed-size state updated sequentially, achieving linear-cost computation and constant-memory inference at the expense of random access to its input. Analyses from both directions agree that the toll is real: generalized SSMs are provably weaker than attention at copying and retrieving from context (Jelassi et al., 2024), and despite their recurrent form they inherit expressiveness limits similar to attentions own (Merrill et al., 2024). For embedding models, this trade-off is particularly acute: rerankers bind query tokens to candidate tokens, instruction-conditioned encoders retain the prompt information until the readout, and dense encoders must settle token-level correspondence through all-to-all contextual disambiguation before poolingall content-addressable lookups that fixed-size state approximates poorly. Linear attention marks the middle ground: rewriting attention with kernel feature maps turns the quadratic operator into constant-memory, linear-time recurrence (Katharopoulos et al., 2020), lineage that runs through RWKV and RetNets retention (Peng et al., 2023; Sun et al., 2023b); and the structured state-space duality result shows SSMs and attention variants to be closely related decompositions of one matrix class (Dao & Gu, 2024), so the practical question is less which family wins than where each belongs. For the models this survey tracks, the answer still favors the Transformer: the interaction and recall on which embedding quality leans are exactly what the state space family sacrifices to achieve its efficiency, and that efficiency is decisive only where sequence length rather than association is the binding constraintraw audio, video, and genomic sequences at lengths attention cannot afford. The SSM wave is therefore best read not as counterexample but as second demonstration of this chapters argument: the convergence runs deeper than either backbone, toward modality-agnostic token processors that leverage per-modality tokenizers and injected structural priors. 4.3 Modality-Specific Architectures as Inductive Biases Reading the above as the Transformer wins everywhere would be premature. The modalityspecific architecturesCNNs, GNNs, RNNsare best understood not as inferior predecessors but as encodings of strong domain priors the Transformer omits, and there are regimes where those priors remain advantageous. CNNs encode translation equivariance and locality. convolutions shared weights and local receptive field are the prior that helps vision in low-data regimes (Krizhevsky et al., 2012; Long et al., 2015); group-equivariant and steerable CNNs make those symmetries explicit (Cohen & Welling, 2016; 2017; Cohen et al., 2018). GNNs encode prescribed topology. Message-passing over fixed graph is the inductive bias that lets GNNs respect graph structure by construction (Kipf & Welling, 2017; Velickovic et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2026a). Graph Transformers reuse attention as an operator but are 22 Omnimodal Embeddings graph mechanisms only when relational structure is encoded into tokenization, attention bias, positional signal, edge representation, or training taskthey are alternative routes for exposing structure to sequence-style architectures, not structure-free replacements for message passing (Ying et al., 2021; Yuan et al., 2026). Code encoders inject program structure as pluggable prior. Code demonstrates the plugin pattern at the level of the input and the attention mask: the same Transformer backbone becomes structure-aware once its inputs and masks carry data-flow or AST structure with them. GraphCodeBERT (Guo et al., 2021) augments code and text tokens with data-flow nodes guided by graph attention masks constructed from data-flow and source-token relations; and UniXcoder (Guo et al., 2022) linearizes the AST into the token stream. Code thus supplies the sharpest worked example of the core mechanism plus pluggable structural priors recipe: the backbone is untouched, but its inputs and attention masks carry programs syntax and semantics instead of raw surface tokens. RNNs and TCNs encode temporal recurrence. Recurrence and causal convolutions carry the sequential prior useful for time series in small-data regimes; the asynchronous (point-process) regime still relies on continuous-time LSTMs and attention over event sets (Mei & Eisner, 2017; Mei et al., 2022). The state space family of Section 4.2 is this bullets modern descendant: the recurrence prior made parallelizable, and scaled until it too could claim backbone status. The right framing is therefore trade-off, not verdict: strong inductive biases buy data efficiency and low-data performance but limit expressiveness, while the Transformers weak bias buys generality and scalability at the cost of being data-hungry. Nor is the contest one-dimensionala counter-current even within time series argues that attention is not always the right primitive: TSLANets adaptive spectral filtering at O(N log N) beats Transformers in small-data, high-noise regimes (Eldele et al., 2024), and single linear layer matches elaborate Transformers on longhorizon forecasting (Zeng et al., 2023). Both are the expected consequence of trade-off in which the modalitys data, scale, and priors jointly determine which architecture dominates. The convergence is toward default: the Transformer is the first choice when data and compute are ample, and modality-specific architectures remain the right tool when priors are strong and data are scarce. Beyond the backbone: interaction architectures. Two further architectural choices recur across modalities and set up Sections 7 and 8. The dual-encoder (bi-encoder) encodes query and candidate independently and compares them in embedding space, enabling approximate nearest-neighbor search at scale, while the cross-encoder fuses query and candidate with full cross-attention for higher accuracy at the cost of one joint forward pass per querycandidate pair, and is used as reranker over dual-encoder shortlist (Nogueira et al., 2020; Zhuang et al., 2023). The dual-encoder is the architecture of alignment (Section 7); the cross-encoder, generalized to multiple modalities, is an architecture for fusion (Section 8). Finally, given Transformers hidden states (h1, . . . , hL), the embedding must be reduced by pooling[CLS], mean, attention, or the last token for causal models. The choice of pooling interacts with the representational object of Section 2.2: vision model that keeps its set of patch vectors (Faysse et al., 2025) or an audio model that keeps sequence of frame features (Baevski et al., 2020) deliberately refuses global pooling, trading efficiency for the dense correspondence that downstream tasks need. Takeaway The Transformer converges as the default universal encoder not by eliminating inductive biases, but by adopting minimal, set-based operator whose missing structural priors (order, lattice, topology) are re-injected via modality-specific tokenizers and positional encodings. While emerging state space models share this tokenized interface, their fixed-size states sacrifice the all-to-all contextual resolution and recall essential for fine-grained retrieval representations. Meanwhile, modality-specific architectures (CNNs, GNNs) remain principled choices rather than outdated predecessors, offering vital data efficiency in strong-prior, data-scarce regimes. 23 Omnimodal Embeddings

sections.title: 5 Data and Representational Objects: Units, Granularity, and the Upward Shift
sections.content: The third axis of convergence is that the granularity at which each modality assigns its embeddings is moving upwardfrom tokens and pixels toward sentences, images, clips, graphs, and events. Where Section 3 found convergence in the loss and Section 4 in the encoder, this chapter finds it in the representational object: across every modality the field is choosing to encode whole semantic units rather than their parts, and the consequences of that choice are the focus of this chapter: what it preserves, what it discards, and where it is reversed. We unpack it in two steps: first the distinction between the input data unit and the output representational object, which is the key to understanding how modalities differ even as their encoders converge (Section 5.1), and then the upward granularity shift itself, which is the corresponding verb of Part II (Section 5.2). 5.1 Units and Representational Objects subtlety that the convergence analysis must keep in view is the separation of the model input from the extracted output. The data unit is the atom of the input: the subword, the patch, the spectrogram frame, the node, the cell, and the timestamp at which an encoder first sees the signal. The representational object is the atom of the outputthe entity at which an embedding is actually assigned and which downstream consumers retrieve, compare, and combine. The two are not the same, and the gap between them is where modalitys structure lives: pixel is unit of input, but the entity assigned an embedding is modeling choice (Rust et al., 2023); an audio frame is unit of input, but request to embed an utterance is incomplete until the factor to be keptcontent, speaker, or emotionis named. Raw inputs such as pixels are physical measurements, and the choice of representational object is modeling commitment to which information must survive the interface and which may be discarded (Lin et al., 2024). The input data unit is set by what each modality can plausibly carve up, and the granularity of that unit trades off resolution against sequence length: finer carving preserves more detail but lengthens the sequence the encoder must process. The families supply different candidate units. Text and code have characters, subwords, tokens, and spans, with boundaries partly supplied by symbolic system. Vision offers pixels, patches, regions, and frames. Audio has waveform samples, spectrogram frames, and continuous latent frames. Time series provides timestamped samples, channels, windows, and patches, but its semantically useful window and even its series boundary can be task-dependent. Graph methods ingest nodes, edges, typed triples, paths, or subgraphs (Bordes et al., 2013; Perozzi et al., 2014; Ying et al., 2021; Khoshraftar & An, 2024). Tables offer cells, rows, and columns. recurring difficulty is that the unit is often manufactured choice, not given one: no pixel is persistent semantic identity across images; an audio frame is not an object the way word is; sampled time-series value has no meaning without its variable, unit, instrument, scale, and timestamp (Yue et al., 2022; Nie et al., 2023).
