Zhang et al., 2025c) Visionlanguage and combinations retrieval Negative sampling by modality and fused training P Does not test arbitrary input subsets UniME-V2 et al., 2026) (Gu Universal visionlanguage embedding tasks Model-generated semantic supervision P Richer supervision; evaluation remains limited to vision and language OmniRet et al., 2026) (Huynh Textvisionaudio combined queries SOLAR (Yang et al., 2026) Imagetext combinations on both sides and Resampling attention-slicedWasserstein pooling Shared/private masking and joint vectors OmniUE et al., 2026b) (Wang Text, image, video, audio, regions and spans Omni-LLM interactive embeddings P Three media types, but only some combinations Both retrieval roles, but only two modalities Many prompt formats; no independent benchmark replication at the cutoff DME (Chen et al., 2026c) Queries over images, videos and visual documents Evidence-grounded latent serving vector reasoning; one Full composition tests and serving details are not public the least established capability: todays models cover many inputs and increasingly match them pairwise, but reliable evidence that an output genuinely depends on multiple inputs is thin and almost entirely confined to visionlanguage. Takeaway We cannot build what we cannot measure. Existing frozen-encoder benchmarks remain isolated islands: they reliably certify coverage (C1) and pairwise comparability (C2), but almost entirely overlook compositionality (C3)the defining test of true joint fusion. Because multimodal evaluation easily admits unimodal shortcuts and data licensing bottlenecks, evaluating genuine compositional gain (comp) across all modalities remains unresolved. Until unified, decoder-independent benchmark exists, the thesis that joint embedding unifies and surpasses alignment remains compelling hypothesis rather than an established empirical fact.

sections.title: 12 Conclusion and Future Outlook
sections.content: We have traced the trajectory of embedding research from fragmentation to fusion. The field began as separate continentstext, vision, audio, graph, table, and time series, each with its own research community, its own surveys, and its own benchmarks (Section 1). Beneath this fragmentation, four 57 Omnimodal Embeddings trends quietly converged: contrastive learning became the lingua franca, the Transformer became the universal encoder, the pretrainfinetune paradigm standardized training, and the representational granularity shifted from parts to whole semantic units (Sections 3 to 5). That convergence, we argued, is not coincidence but evidence of deeper alignment toward shared platonic representation of reality, in which single geometry underlies embeddings across modalities (Huh et al., 2024; Jha et al., 2025). The path to unification, we showed, has three steps. Transformation (Section 6) unifies by discarding differences, rendering modalities as images or serializing them as text, at the cost of structural information loss. Alignment (Section 7) unifies by aligning separately encoded spaces, and suffers from the modality gap that the contrastive cone effect and the dual-encoder bias make persistent (Liang et al., 2022). Joint embedding (Section 8) unifies by letting modalities interact inside the model, and in principle unifies and surpasses alignment: it is generalization that fuses when the input is multimodal and specializes into strong encoder when it is unimodal, dissolving the artificial boundary between the two, provided training recipes actively mitigate modality interference. But reaching this terminus is not matter of scaling up single model. It requires respecting what is modality-specificthe difference axisrather than dismissing it: texts discreteness and compositionality, visions spatial multi-scale structure, audios superposition of factors, graphs explicit relational structure, tables typed grid geometry and two readings, and time series continuous axis, absent vocabulary, and magnitude semantics (Section 9). And it requires cross-pollinationdirected, conditional ports of method hardened in one modality into another whose preconditions hold, which we map out as concrete opportunity map (Section 10). None of this is measurable without unified, decoder-independent, omnimodal benchmark (Section 11), which is the binding prerequisite for turning the convergence thesis from hypothesis into measured fact. The broader claim is that true omnimodal joint embedding is not merely technical synthesisa single model doing the work of manybut shift in what embedding models are for. Today an embedding is modality-specific interface: text embedding for text retrieval, an image embedding for image retrieval, an alignment between the two. genuine joint embedding is universal representational interface, one space in which any datum of any modality is laid down according to common geometry, retrievable, comparable, and combinable with any other. This is what human intelligence has always done, and it is urgent because omni representation is lagging behind omni generation (Section 1.2), concrete gap this road map exists to close. If the Platonic conjecture holds and shared geometry underlies all modalities, then the omnimodal joint embedding is the model that exposes it, and its completion may be key stepping-stone toward more general forms of machine intelligence that perceive the world not modality by modality, but whole. 58 Omnimodal Embeddings Per-Modality Cheat Sheets This section includes cheat sheets for readers who want quick orientation in single modalitys history and milestones without interrupting the concept-first main thread. For each modality we first record the static anatomy of Sections 2 and 5the data objects, units, and granularities it offers; the backbone and inductive bias that suit it; the recurring objectives; and the interfaces or exposed embedding object it servesand then the developmental arc, list of milestone modeling works, separate list of evaluation benchmarks, and pointer to where the modality enters the cross-modal argument. A.1 Text Figure 8: Development history of text embeddings. Data objects, units, and granularities. Subwords, tokens, spans, clauses, sentences, paragraphs, and documents; boundaries are partly supplied by symbol system. The favored representational object shifts upward toward the sentence and the document (Section 5), with the token sequence retained as local object when grounding is needed. Backbone and inductive bias. Encoder-only Transformers and, increasingly, causal decoder-only LLMs repurposed as embedders; the only inductive bias beyond attention is positional (and sometimes RoPE/ALiBi) encoding over an ordered token sequence. Objectives. MLM pretraining giving way to contrastive finetuning (SimCSE, DPR), contrastive training with role prefixes (E5), and natural-language instruction conditioning (INSTRUCTOR, E5-Mistral). Next-token prediction joins as hybrid head (GRIT) and decoder-only generative pretraining as pretext for embedders. Interfaces / exposed object. single global sentence/document vector for retrieval is the default; multi-vector or late-interaction readouts (ColBERT-style) retain the local token sequence for grounding, and instruction-conditioned interfaces expose task-aware vector. Omnimodal Embeddings Arc. Static word vectors contextual representations contrastive finetuning task-aware (instruction) embeddings decoder-only LLMs as embedders. Modeling milestones. Static word vectors: word2vec (Mikolov et al., 2013), GloVe (Pennington et al., 2014), fastText (Bojanowski et al., 2017) Contextual & BERT-based & contrastive embeddings: USE (Cer et al., 2018), ELMo (Peters et al., 2018), BERT (Devlin et al., 2019), RoBERTa (Liu et al., 2019), SpanBERT (Joshi et al., 2020), ALBERT (Lan et al., 2020), TinyBERT (Jiao et al., 2020), DistilBERT (Sanh et al., 2019), XLM-R (Conneau et al., 2020), MiniLM (Wang et al., 2020), ELECTRA (Clark et al., 2020), MobileBERT (Sun et al., 2020b), DeBERTa (He et al., 2021; 2023), SBERT (Reimers & Gurevych, 2019), DPR (Karpukhin et al., 2020), ColBERT (Khattab & Zaharia, 2020; Santhanam et al., 2022), SimCSE (Gao et al., 2021), Sentence-T5 (Ni et al., 2022a), GTR (Ni et al., 2022b), Contriever (Izacard et al., 2022), E5 (Wang et al., 2022a; 2024c), INSTRUCTOR (Su et al., 2023), GTE (Li et al., 2023g; Zhang et al., 2024d), BGE (Xiao et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2024b), Jina Embedding v1-3 (Günther et al., 2023a;b; Sturua et al., 2024), Nomic Embed (Nussbaum et al., 2025), Arctic-Embed (Merrick et al., 2024), ModernBERT (Warner et al., 2025), NeoBERT (Breton et al., 2025), mmBERT (Marone et al., 2025), LateOn (Sourty et al., 2026) LLM-based embeddings: cpt (Neelakantan et al., 2022), SGPT (Muennighoff, 2022), PromptEOL (Jiang et al., 2024a), E5-Mistral (Wang et al., 2024d), GRIT (Muennighoff et al., 2025), Echo (Springer et al., 2025), NV-Embed (Lee et al., 2025a), LLM2Vec (BehnamGhader et al., 2024), D2LLM (Liao et al., 2024), Gemini Embedding (Lee et al., 2025b), KaLM-Embedding (Zhao et al., 2025b), Qwen3-Embedding (Zhang et al., 2025d), Conan-Embedding (Li et al., 2025c), F2LLM (Zhang et al., 2025e), F2LLM-v2 (Zhang et al., 2026b), ML-Embed (Zhang et al., 2026c) Evaluation benchmarks. The text community built the canonical frozen-encoder instrument: MTEB (Muennighoff et al., 2023), its retrieval focus BEIR (Thakur et al., 2021) and AIRBench (Chen et al., 2025b), the reasoning-intensive BRIGHT (Su et al., 2025), and the multilingual MMTEB (Enevoldsen et al., 2025). Beyond English, the MTEB recipe has been re-instantiated per language, each surfacing where general (often English-centric) embedders fail: C-MTEB for Chinese (Xiao et al., 2023), MTEB-French (Ciancone et al., 2024), the Scandinavian Embedding Benchmark (Danish, Swedish, Norwegian) (Enevoldsen et al., 2024), ruMTEB for Russian (Snegirev et al., 2025), FaMTEB for Persian (Zinvandi et al., 2025), VN-MTEB for Vietnamese (Pham et al., 2026), MTEB-NL for Dutch (Banar et al., 2026), and German text-embedding clustering benchmark (Wehrli et al., 2023). Cross-modal pointers. Contrastive intersection (Section 3.1); LLM-as-encoder and pooling (Section 4); instruction tuning as cross-pollination export (Section 10); polysemy and anisotropy as difference (Section 9); MTEB/MMTEB evaluation silos (Section 11). A.2 Code Data objects, units, and granularities. Tokens, statements, blocks, methods, files, modules, projects; an attested hierarchical structure (the AST and the data-flow graph) sits above the surface text. The current frontier exposes intermediate-representation units (LLVM IR) that are behaviorand machine-independent. Backbone and inductive bias. Transformer encoders with pluggable structural prior: GraphCodeBERT injects data-flow adjacency as an attention mask, UniXcoder linearizes the AST into the token stream. Inductive bias is supplied by these structure-bearing inputs and masks, not by the Transformer backbone itself (Section 4.3). 60 Omnimodal Embeddings Figure 9: Development history of code embeddings. Objectives. Bimodal masked prediction and replaced-token detection (CodeBERT) identifieraware and structure-aware masked targets (GraphCodeBERT, CodeT5) contrastive codecode / codetext views (CodeRetriever, CODE-MVP, CodeSage) executionand trace-grounded contrastive pretraining (fuzz pretraining). Interfaces / exposed object. global function/method vector for code search dominates; the AST/data-flow structure is relational view and not by itself the served object, so the typical interface is single code vector, occasionally with instruction conditioning. Arc. General-purpose BERT on code bimodal NL-PL pretraining structure-aware (data-flow / AST / multi-view) pretraining unified encoder-decoder models retrieval-focused contrastive code embeddings Code-LLM-based embedders. Each era asks what structure of code should the representation preserve? and answers it one layer deeper each time: surface tokens, syntax, semantics, behavior (Zhang et al., 2024f). Modeling milestones. Figure 9 summarizes 34 representative works; the milestones below group them by the layer of code structure they set out to preservethe question the Arc above answers one era deeper each time. Static structural embeddings (pre-pretraining): CODEnn (Gu et al., 2018) (joint NLcode embedding for code search: LSTM max-pooled method-name, API-call, and body features aligned with descriptions), code2vec (Alon et al., 2019b) and code2seq (Alon et al., 2019a) (AST path-contexts as the unit, with attention over sampled paths) Masked, bimodal, and structure-aware pretraining: CuBERT (Kanade et al., 2020) (BERT for Python), CodeBERT (Feng et al., 2020) (bimodal PL+NL with replaced-token detection), TreeBERT (Jiang et al., 2021) (the AST serialized as composition paths and trained with tree masked language modeling plus node order prediction), GraphCodeBERT (Guo et al., 2021) (data-flow structure; edge prediction and code-structure alignment), SynCoBERT (Wang et al., 2021a) and CODE-MVP (Wang et al., 2022c) (syntax-/multi-view-contrastive code representations), 61 Omnimodal Embeddings CodeT5 (Wang et al., 2021b) (identifier-aware unified encoder-decoder), PLBART (Ahmad et al., 2021) (denoising-autoencoding seq2seq), UniXcoder (Guo et al., 2022) (cross-modal code+AST+comment with contrastive learning), CodeT5+ (Wang et al., 2023c) (mixture-ofobjectives code LLMs with contrastive learning and text-code matching) Semantics-preserving and cross-language contrastive: ContraCode (Jain et al., 2021) (semantics-preserving compiler transforms as the augmentation that defines functional equivalence), DISCO (Ding et al., 2022) (synthetic clones and injected real-world bugs as program contrasts), and language-agnostic alignment across programming languages (Utpala et al., 2024) Compiler-IR embeddings: IR2Vec builds flow-aware LLVM-IR embeddings that are languageand machine-independent (VenkataKeerthy et al., 2020), and IRGen shows that joint training over source code and LLVM IR improves clone-detection embeddings beyond source-only CodeBERT (Li et al., 2022c) Execution-grounded pretraining: FuzzPretrain uses fuzzer-generated inputoutput test cases as dynamic complements and distills the behavior signal into code-only features (Huang et al., 2024a) Retrieval-focused contrastive embedders: CodeRetriever (Li et al., 2022b), CodeSage (Zhang et al., 2024a), the code variant of Jina Embedding v2 (Günther et al., 2023b), and CodeRankEmbed (Suresh et al., 2025) Code-LLM-based embedders: StarEncoder (Li et al., 2023e) (the encoder-only model of the StarCoder family), CodeXEmbed (Liu et al., 2024b), CodeR (Li et al., 2025a), Jina-code (Kryvosheieva et al., 2025), and C2LLM (Qin et al., 2025) Evaluation benchmarks. CodeSearchNet (Husain et al., 2019) originated large-scale NLcode search (6M functions, 6 languages), and CodeXGLUE (Lu et al., 2021) consolidated code intelligence into 10-task / 14-dataset benchmark (code search, clone detection, defect detection, completion, translation, summarization), and CoSQA (Huang et al., 2021a) added 20K+ human-annotated web search queries paired with code for search and question answering. The recent MTEB-style frozen-encoder suite for code retrieval is CoIR (Li et al., 2025e), with CPRet (Deng et al., 2025) for competitive programming and CoREB (Xue et al., 2026a) extending the pipeline. Cross-modal pointers. Replaced-token detection and identifier-aware objectives as reconstructive difference (Section 3.2); contrastive NL-PL alignment and zero-shot code-to-code search (Section 3.1, Section 7); structure-aware encoders as strong-prior architecture (Section 4.3); executable semantics, cross-language equivalence, and hierarchy as the code-specific difference (Section 9); codec/trace discretization and graph structural modeling as cross-pollination targets (Section 10); the CoIR/CoREB evaluation silo (Section 11). A.3 Table Data objects, units, and granularities. Cell, header/type, row, column, and whole table; the affine 2D grid geometry is itself part of the semantics. Unlike most modalities, all three granularities (cell, row, column) are legitimate representational objects, and the chosen grain is task-dependent TABBIE deliberately exposes all three. Backbone and inductive bias. Structure-aware encoders inject the strong prior that cells meaning depends on its value, its column type, and its row, but they do so differently: TABBIE runs two Transformers over the rows and the columns to recover the 2D grid that flat serialization would hide; TaPas keeps flat serialization and re-attaches the grid through explicit row and column index embeddings; and FT-Transformer, on the tabular-ML reading, tokenizes each feature of single row with feature-specific parameters before attending across features. The inductive bias is strong enough that shared text backbone fed serialized column=value string underperforms structure-aware encoder. 62 Omnimodal Embeddings Figure 10: Development history of tabular embeddings. Objectives. Masked entity recovery over web tables (TURL), corrupt-cell detection (TABBIE), masked tabletext pretraining (masked language, column, and cell-value prediction in TaBERT; masked language modeling over text and table cells in TaPas), cross-row intersample contrast (SAINT); the ML reading prefers representation-learning objective that mirrors TabPFN-style in-context prediction. Interfaces / exposed object. From single global table vector, to per-cell / per-row / per-column vectors that let consumers query at their own grain (TABBIE); the document reading serves global or row-level vector for QA and retrieval, the ML reading row embedding for supervised prediction. The same artifact thus supports two served objects. Arc. Tables sit on fault line between two readings that the field has never fully reconciled: tablesas-semi-structured documents (a 2D layout of typed cells with headers, captions, and rowcolumn geometry, the natural unit for retrieval and question answering) and tabular ML data (i.i.d. feature rows, the natural unit for prediction). The document thread runs from serializing tables into BERT structure-aware table encoders (rowcolumn attention) table-text joint pretraining table retrieval-augmentation; the ML thread runs from feature engineering tabular deep models in-context tabular foundation models. Modeling milestones (documents). On the document thread: Tablelanguage pretraining: TaBERT (Yin et al., 2020) (joint NL+table pretraining over 26M tables), TaPas (Herzig et al., 2020) (BERT extended with table row/column embeddings for weakly-supervised QA), TURL (Deng et al., 2020) (structure-aware Transformer with Masked Entity Recovery objective for web tables), TABBIE (Iida et al., 2021) (two bidirectional Transformers over rows and columns, corrupt-cell-detection objective; embeds cells, rows, and columns), TAPEX (Liu et al., 2022a) (table pretraining by learning neural SQL executor over the linearized table) 63 Omnimodal Embeddings Table LLMs and retrieval augmentation: TableLlama (Zhang et al., 2024c) (an open table LLM trained over large corpus of serialized tables), TableRAG (Chen et al., 2024e) (schema + cell retrieval over million-token tables) Modeling milestones (tabular ML). On the ML thread: Supervised deep tabular encoders: TabNet (Arik & Pfister, 2021) (attention-based sequential feature selection across decision steps, with self-supervised pretext phase for unlabeled data), TabTransformer (Huang et al., 2020) (self-attention over categorical column embeddings while numerical features bypass the Transformerthe direct precursor of the feature-tokenizer line), FT-Transformer (Gorishniy et al., 2021) (feature-tokenizer + Transformer, supervised deep baseline that embeds all columns) Self-supervised tabular pretraining: VIME (Yoon et al., 2020) (mask-vector estimation plus masked feature reconstruction from corrupted inputs), SAINT (Somepalli et al., 2021) (intrarow and intersample attention with contrastive tabular pretraining), SubTab (Ucar et al., 2021) (feature subsetting as the multi-view augmentation, reconstructing the full row from each subset), HyTrel (Chen et al., 2023b) (tables as hypergraphs whose row, column, and wholetable hyperedges yield cell, row, column, and table embeddings), SwitchTab (Wu et al., 2024a) (autoencoders that split each row embedding into sample-specific and shared part, switching the shared parts across training samples), UniTabE (Yang et al., 2024b) (a universal cell-level mask-then-predict protocol over TabUnits, pretrained on roughly 13B Kaggle rows) In-context tabular foundation models: TabPFN (Hollmann et al., 2023) and TabPFN v2 (Hollmann et al., 2025) (prior-data fitted networks: in-context tabular prediction, not reusable embedding), TabICL (Qu et al., 2025) (column-then-row attention that scales in-context prediction to hundreds of thousands of rows) Evaluation benchmarks. Document-thread tables are scored on QA / semantic-parsing tasks rather than frozen-encoder embedding suite: WikiTableQuestions (Pasupat & Liang, 2015), WikiSQL (Zhong et al., 2017) (80K crowdsourced questionSQL pairs over 24K Wikipedia tablesthe corpus that launched neural text-to-SQL), Spider (Yu et al., 2018) (text-to-SQL), TabFact (Chen et al., 2020c) (table fact verification), ToTTo (Parikh et al., 2020) (controlled table-to-text), and TAT-QA (Zhu et al., 2021a) (hybrid table+text QA in finance); TableRAG adds retrieval-recall benchmarks at million-token scale (ArcadeQA, BirdQA (Chen et al., 2024e)), and Table Meets LLM (Sui et al., 2024) shows that no serialization format (markdown, JSON, or others) is uniformly dominant for LLM consumption. Only very recently has the MTEB recipe started to reach tables: TEmBed probes frozen tabular encoders at cell/row/column/table level across 69 datasets (Vogel et al., 2026), TabBench (with the TabEmbed model) evaluates frozen general-purpose embedders on tabular classification and row retrieval (Qiang et al., 2026), and TRL-Bench wraps twenty heterogeneous tabular encoders in one shared embedding interface probed by lightweight heads (Pang et al., 2026). Tabular ML has otherwise been scored by prediction accuracy (the OpenML/TabPFN evaluation regime), flagging the same decoder-coupling gap as time series. recent survey formalizes the specialized/transferable/general tiers of tabular representation learning (Jiang et al., 2026). Cross-modal pointers. Serializing tables as text (Section 6.2); rowcolumn structural encoding as strong-prior architecture (Section 4.3); table-cell discretization and the only-now-emerging frozen-encoder instruments (Section 11); semi-structured layout as modality-specific difference (Section 9); column-type and relational structure as cross-pollination export to graphs and documents (Section 10). A. Image and Video Data objects, units, and granularities. Pixels, patches, regions, objects, frames, tracks, clips, and events; most identities above the pixel are inferred rather than given. The grain moves upward 64 Omnimodal Embeddings Figure 11: Development history of visual embeddings. from patches to whole images, but dense and region-level features are retained where grounding, correspondence, or motion is needed. Backbone and inductive bias. ViTs (patchify + project) became the default descriptor; 3D-conv patch embeddings handle video tubelets. The inductive bias CNNs encoded (translation equivariance and locality) is omitted by the ViT, which retains only the local patch projection and learned positional encodings, the textbook weak prior plus pluggable position of Section 4.1. Objectives. Contrastive at the image level (SimCLR, CLIP), self-distillation (DINO), redundancy reduction (Barlow Twins, VICReg), masked reconstruction of continuous pixels (MAE), token-level contrast in early-fusion ViTs. The contrastive and reconstructive families now coexist; generative VQ objectives (VQ-VAE, MAGVIT-v2) build discrete visual codes for generation. Interfaces / exposed object. One global vector for retrieval and zero-shot classification is the canonical interface; the local patch set is preserved by dense and late-interaction models (ColPali) for fine-grained document retrieval, and equivariance-aware variants keep set of per-object embeddings. Video adds the temporal axis on top of an image appearance model. Arc. Bag-of-visual-words learned CNN features instance discrimination masked reconstruction image-level contrast and CLIP multimodal/dense representations; video adds temporal axis and hierarchy of units. Figure 11 summarizes 55 representative works. Modeling milestones. Engineered local descriptors: Video Google (Sivic & Zisserman, 2003) (bag-of-visual-words retrieval), SIFT (Lowe, 2004), Fisher vectors (Perronnin et al., 2010), and VLAD (Jégou et al., 2010), which aggregate local descriptors into compact global codes Supervised CNN features and readouts: AlexNet (Krizhevsky et al., 2012), DeCAF (Donahue et al., 2014) (frozen-CNN features as transferable vectors), ResNet (He et al., 2016); FCN (Long 65 Omnimodal Embeddings et al., 2015) and DETR (Carion et al., 2020) exposed dense and object-level readouts of such features, DETRs learned object queries serving as detection embeddings Instance retrieval and metric learning: FaceNet (Schroff et al., 2015) (triplet-trained identity vectors), Product-VQ (Wu & Flierl, 2019) (a product quantizer in the VQ-VAE bottleneck, so retrieval runs on sub-codeword distance lookups), Loc-VAE (Nishimaki et al., 2022) (a β-VAE whose latent dimensions localize to brain regions, for medical image retrieval) ViT and self-supervised pretraining: ViT (Dosovitskiy et al., 2021) (the patch-token interface), MoCo (He et al., 2020), SimCLR (Chen et al., 2020b), SwAV (Caron et al., 2020) (predicting cluster assignments instead of pairwise comparison), BYOL (Grill et al., 2020), Barlow Twins (Zbontar et al., 2021) and VICReg (Bardes et al., 2022) (negative-free redundancy reduction), DINO (Caron et al., 2021), iBOT (Zhou et al., 2021), BEiT (Bao et al., 2022a) (masked prediction against learned discrete codebook), I-JEPA (Assran et al., 2023) (prediction moved into latent space), MAE (He et al., 2022), DINOv2 (Oquab et al., 2024); at the scaling frontier, Web-SSL (Fan et al., 2025) shows image-only self-supervision on 2B-sample web corpusno language signal at allcan match language-aligned pretraining, DINOv3 (Siméoni et al., 2026) couples web-scale curation with Gram anchoring that keeps patch-level features from degrading during long training runs, AIMv2 (Fini et al., 2025) supervises visual encoder solely through multimodal autoregressive prediction, and D-iGPT (Ren et al., 2024) rejuvenates autoregressive iGPT by predicting semantic tokens from frozen CLIP teacher Quantized and generative visual codes: VQ-VAE (van den Oord et al., 2017), VQGAN (Esser et al., 2021), MAGVIT-v2 (Yu et al., 2024) (lookup-free quantization and causal 3D tokenizer whose codes let language models beat diffusion on image and video generation); the parallel generative-latent lineVAE (Kingma & Welling, 2014), BiGAN/BGAN (Donahue et al., 2017; Song et al., 2018), latent diffusion (Rombach et al., 2022), diffusion autoencoders (Preechakul et al., 2022), DIFT (Tang et al., 2023), and the REPA/MergeVQ representationgeneration convergence (Yu et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025d)is surveyed in Section 3.3, with Chameleon (Team, 2024) interleaving text and visual tokens in one autoregressive stream Video encoders: two-stream (Simonyan & Zisserman, 2014), iDT (Wang & Schmid, 2013) (camera-motion-compensated dense trajectories), C3D (Tran et al., 2015), I3D (Carreira & Zisserman, 2017), SlowFast (Feichtenhofer et al., 2019), TimeSformer (Bertasius et al., 2021) (divided spacetime attention), ViViT (Arnab et al., 2021) Video self-supervision and foundation encoders: VideoMAE (Tong et al., 2022), VideoMAE V2 (Wang et al., 2023a) (dual masking that scales masked video modeling to millions of videos), V-JEPA (Bardes et al., 2024), V-JEPA 2 (Assran et al., 2025) (masked latent prediction on more than million hours of video, with an action-conditioned world model that plans zero-shot on robots), VideoPrism (Zhao et al., 2024) (contrastive pretraining followed by masked video modeling that distills teachers global and token embeddings, one frozen encoder for 30-plus video benchmarks) Videolanguage pretraining for retrieval: HowTo100M (Miech et al., 2019) (100M narrated video clips), Frozen in Time (Bain et al., 2021) (a joint videoimage encoder for end-to-end textvideo retrieval), Everything at Once (Shvetsova et al., 2022), InternVideo2 (Wang et al., 2024f) (joint videotext pretraining scaled to billion-parameter regimes) Cross-modal alignment and joint interfaces: DeViSE (Frome et al., 2013), TIRG (Vo et al., 2019), CLIP (Radford et al., 2021), PCME (Chun et al., 2021), Pic2Word (Saito et al., 2023), CLIPPO (Tschannen et al., 2023), ImageBind (Girdhar et al., 2023), ColPali (Faysse et al., 2025) (late interaction over document patch tokens), VLM2Vec (Jiang et al., 2025); the many-modality and instruction-conditioned successors (Meta-Transformer (Zhang et al., 2023c), 4M-21 (Bachmann et al., 2024), VISTA (Zhou et al., 2024b), UniIR (Wei et al., 2024a), MM-Embed (Lin et al., 2025), GME (Zhang et al., 2025c), UniME (Gu et al., 2025)) are treated as fusion-era works in Section Evaluation benchmarks. Vision lacks single MTEB-analog; instead it relies on task-specific suitesclassification on ImageNet (Russakovsky et al., 2015) (the frozen-encoder linear/zero-shot 66 Omnimodal Embeddings probe), instance-level image retrieval on ROxford/RParis with the Easy/Medium/Hard protocols (Radenovic et al., 2018), and increasingly the multimodal embedding benchmark MMEB (Jiang et al., 2025; Meng et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2026a). Cross-modal pointers. Rendering text as pixels, VisionTS as transformation (Section 6); CLIP/ImageBind alignment hub (Section 7); spatial multi-scale as difference (Section 9); diffusion latents in hybrid objectives (Section 3.3); continuous-time index as an import (Section 10). A.5 Audio Figure 12: Development history of audio embeddings. Data objects, units, and granularities. Samples, frames, phones, spoken-word segments, utterances, speakers, clips, events, tracks, stems. The content layer has an attested recurring inventory (phones, syllables, words) when speech or music is tied to an external symbol system; the factor layer (content vs. speaker vs. prosody vs. environment) is superposed rather than hierarchical, so the chosen grain depends on the factor being asked for. Backbone and inductive bias. Conformers and transformers dominate SSL, with speech models reading temporal feature sequence from convolutional encoder over the raw waveform and general-audio encoders patchifying the timefrequency spectrogram into 2D tokensso grid geometry and sampling rate are inductive biases supplied by the front end. Statistics pooling over frames in the speaker branch (x-vector, ECAPA-TDNN) deliberately keeps the second moments that text-side global pooling would erase. Objectives. Self-supervised masked prediction over quantized targets (wav2vec 2.0, HuBERT), contrastive audiocaption alignment (CLAP), waveform codec discretization into acoustic tokens (SoundStream, EnCodec) and semantic distillation into dedicated codebook (SpeechTokenizer), and removal/anonymization objectives that certify factor is absent. 67 Omnimodal Embeddings Interfaces / exposed object. The defining no single object case: speech-recognition readout is sequence of contextual frame representations, speaker embedding is an utterance-level global vector, codec is discrete code sequence, and dense frame set is local object. The interface must name the factor or expose layer-weighted combination (the SUPERB weighted-sum-over-layers choice). Arc. Generative factor analysis (i-vector) discriminative speaker vectors self-supervised masked prediction over discovered units discrete codec tokens audio-language alignment; four eras that superseded one another cleanly because benchmark (SUPERB) could register the improvement. Modeling milestones. Figure 12 summarizes 38 representative works; the milestones below group them by the factor and interface they serve. Speaker vectors: i-vector (Dehak et al., 2011), d-vector (Variani et al., 2014), x-vector (Snyder et al., 2018), ECAPA-TDNN (Desplanques et al., 2020) Self-supervised speech models: wav2vec 2.0 (Baevski et al., 2020), HuBERT (Hsu et al., 2021), WavLM (Chen et al., 2022a), data2vec (Baevski et al., 2022), DinoSR (Liu et al., 2023a) (online clustering replaces HuBERTs offline k-means with machine-discovered, phone-like targets), EH-MAM (Seth et al., 2024) (easy-to-hard curriculum masking that shifts masking toward frames teacher-predicted loss deems hard) General-audio encoders: PANNs (Kong et al., 2020) (supervised CNNs pretrained on AudioSet and widely reused as frozen feature extractors), AudioMAE (Huang et al., 2022a), BEATs (Chen et al., 2023c), M2D (Niizumi et al., 2023) (the online network predicts the representations of masked patches while the target network encodes only the masked patches, so both are pushed to model the input) Neural codecs and discrete units: SoundStream (Zeghidour et al., 2022), EnCodec (Défossez et al., 2023), SpeechTokenizer (Zhang et al., 2023b) (distilling HuBERT semantics into dedicated codebook), RepCodec (Huang et al., 2024b) (vector-quantizing pretrained speech representations into semantic tokens), Language-Codec (Ji et al., 2025) (fewer codebooks so speech LMs consume fewer tokens), HASRD (Hussein et al., 2025) (an RVQ hierarchy whose first codebook carries the semantic representation and later ones the acoustic residuals), EnCodecMAE (Pepino et al., 2025) (masked prediction of codec token indices as universal-audio objective) Audiolanguage alignment: CLAP (Elizalde et al., 2023) and LAION-CLAP (Wu et al., 2023b), T-CLAP (Yuan et al., 2024) (caption pairs that flip event order to teach temporal structure), M2D-CLAP (Niizumi et al., 2025) (masked modeling and contrastive alignment in one model), GLAP (Dinkel et al., 2025) (one contrastive space across speech, sound events, and music in many languages), Human-CLAP (Takano et al., 2025) (trained against human relevance ratings rather than caption identity), EnCLAP (Kim et al., 2024a) (codec tokens plus CLAP embedding feeding caption decoder) Music representations: MERT (Li et al., 2024) (masked prediction with both codec-token and CQT teachers at 160K-hour scale), Stem-JEPA (Riou et al., 2025) (instrument-conditioned latent prediction of target stem for zero-shot stem retrieval), tempo embedding (McCallum et al., 2024) (a learned translation function that maps an embedding to that of its time-stretched version) Disentanglement and privacy: NeuralFA (Lin et al., 2023a), Eta-WavLM (Ruggiero et al., 2025), WavShape (Baser et al., 2025) Evaluation benchmarks. The supervised general-audio era was built on AudioSet (Gemmeke et al., 2017) (2.1M ten-second YouTube clips labeled with 632-class event ontology). Audio converges on the same frozen-encoder protocol as text: SUPERB (Yang et al., 2021) for speech, HEAR (Turian et al., 2021) for general audio, MARBLE (Yuan et al., 2023) for music, AV-SUPERB (Tseng et al., 2024) for audio-visual, the unified X-ARES (Zhang et al., 2025a), the MTEB-style MSEB (Heigold et al., 2025) 68 Omnimodal Embeddings and MAEB (Assadi et al., 2026a), and the self-supervised-speech benchmarking audit (Zaiem et al., 2023). Cross-modal pointers. Factor superposition as the distinctive audio property (Section 9); codec discretization as an import to code/time series and precondition test (Section 10); codec tokens and CLAP in objectives (Section 3); frozen-encoder benchmark protocol adopted for speech/audio (Section 11). A.6 Graph Figure 13: Development history of graph embeddings. Data objects, units, and granularities. Node, edge, typed triple, path, subgraph, whole graph, relational/logical-query record, and graph-conditioned readout; for dynamic graphs, time slice. The relations are part of the represented object, not by-product of order, so the choice of granularity coincides with the choice of question (node similarity vs. graph similarity vs. triple plausibility). Backbone and inductive bias. Message-passing GNNs encode the strong prior of fixed permutation-equivariant topology; Graph Transformers reuse attention but rely on structural encodings, attention biases, or edge features to re-expose the topology (Section 4.3). The inductive bias is therefore in how the graph structure is exposed to the backbone, not in the attention operator itself. Objectives. Random-walk/proximity co-occurrence (DeepWalk, node2vec); typed-relation scoring and triple plausibility (TransE, RotatE); contrastive learning over augmented graph views (GraphCL); masked feature reconstruction (GraphMAE/GraphMAE2); learned structural codes and distillation (VQGraph); and latent prediction (Graph-JEPA). Interfaces / exposed object. Node vectors, triple/entity-relation scores, subgraph and wholegraph readouts, and relation/edge-conditioned objects can each be served; the wrong readout silently answers the wrong question, so the contract must name the represented object and the permutation/visibility assumptions. 69 Omnimodal Embeddings Arc. Graph representation learning develops through overlapping threads: graph-specific proximity and relational scoring, structure-aware encoders, reusable self-supervised representations, and graph foundation models (GFMs) that seek transfer across graphs and tasks. complementary thread aligns graph attributes with language and other modalities. The change is in what can be reused across domains, not necessary progression toward one whole-graph vector. Figure 13 summarizes 51 representative works; the modeling milestones below supply their references. Modeling milestones. DeepWalk (Perozzi et al., 2014), LINE (Tang et al., 2015), node2vec (Grover & Leskovec, 2016), SDNE (Wang et al., 2016), TransE (Bordes et al., 2013), ComplEx (Trouillon et al., 2016), RotatE (Sun et al., 2019), Poincaré embeddings (Nickel & Kiela, 2017), DUPLEX (Ke et al., 2024); GCN (Kipf & Welling, 2017), GraphSAGE (Hamilton et al., 2017), GAT (Velickovic et al., 2018), GIN (Xu et al., 2019), DiffPool (Ying et al., 2018), metapath2vec (Dong et al., 2017), R-GCN (Schlichtkrull et al., 2018), HGT (Hu et al., 2020c), NBFNet (Zhu et al., 2021c), TGAT (Xu et al., 2020a), DySAT (Sankar et al., 2018), Graphormer (Ying et al., 2021), GraphGPS (Rampásek et al., 2022); GNN pretraining (Hu et al., 2020b), DGI (Velickovic et al., 2019), InfoGraph (Sun et al., 2020a), GraphCL (You et al., 2020), MVGRL (Hassani & Ahmadi, 2020), GCA (Zhu et al., 2021b), GraphMAE (Hou et al., 2022), GraphMAE2 (Hou et al., 2023), Graph-JEPA (Skenderi et al., 2025); NodePiece (Galkin et al., 2022), TokenGT (Kim et al., 2022), Mole-BERT (Xia et al., 2023), VQGraph (Yang et al., 2024a); GraphMVP (Liu et al., 2022b), GRENADE (Li et al., 2023f), Edgeformers (Jin et al., 2023a), G2P2 (Wen & Fang, 2023), GLEM (Zhao et al., 2023a), TAPE (He et al., 2024), OFA (Liu et al., 2024a), UniGraph (He et al., 2025a), UniGraph2 (He et al., 2025b), GOFA (Kong et al., 2025); ULTRA (Galkin et al., 2024), Flock (Kim et al., 2025), GFT (Wang et al., 2024h), GraphAny (Zhao et al., 2025a), NodePFN (Choi et al., 2026), GraphBFF (Bechler-Speicher et al., 2026); dynamic: DyG2Vec (Alomrani et al., 2024), TeAST (Li et al., 2023b), STOKE (Gao et al., 2023b), ECOLA (Han et al., 2023), TFLEX (Lin et al., 2023b). Evaluation benchmarks. Evaluation spans several complementary settings: OGB (Hu et al., 2020a) for node, link, and graph-property prediction; MoleculeNet (Wu et al., 2017) for molecular properties; and the Heterogeneous Graph Benchmark (HGB) (Lv et al., 2021) for typed-node and relation settings. Structural stress tests include the Long Range Graph Benchmark (LRGB) (Dwivedi et al., 2022) for long-range dependencies and the heterophily benchmark (Platonov et al., 2023), including Roman-empire and Amazon-ratings, for node classification beyond strongly homophilous graphs. Heterogeneous types and heterophily are distinct axes. For GFM transfer, the text-space benchmark (Chen et al., 2024f) unifies evaluation across graph datasets and tasks, while recent benchmark (Yu et al., 2026) jointly varies topic and format domains through multi-domain pretraining and few-shot adaptation. Cross-modal pointers. Explicit relational structure and non-Euclidean geometry as the distinctive property (Section 9); relational abstraction as an export to text/code (Section 10); message-passing and Graph Transformer as strong-prior architecture (Section 4); contrastive views and triple reconstruction (Section 3); continuous-time machinery shared with time series (Section 10). A.7 Time Series Data objects, units, and granularities. Sample, channel, window, patch, complete series, and timestamped event; the window and even the series boundary are task-dependent, and the recurring units are not standardized across domains (a QRS complex, bearing harmonic, and retail seasonality do not form one vocabulary). Point-process streams add the mark as an attested discrete token set. Backbone and inductive bias. RNN/LSTM encoders carry sequential-recurrence prior while TCNs capture temporal context through dilated causal convolutions; patch Transformers (PatchTST, MOMENT) reuse the text backbone with per-channel patch token, and continuous-time LSTMs / latent ODEs / time-attention add continuous clock. The counter-evidence (TSLANet, DLinear) is that attention is not always the right primitive in small-data, high-noise regimes (Section 4.3). 70 Omnimodal Embeddings Figure 14: Development history of time-series embeddings. Objectives. Contrastive over windows, scales, and timefrequency views (TS2Vec, TF-C); masked patch reconstruction (PatchTST, MOMENT) with the interpolation-pitfall caveat; probabilistic forecasting pretraining (MOIRAI) and LLM-bridging serialization (TEST, LETS-C); declared-symmetry objectives (hard-coded invariances) and magnitude-preserving factorization (NuTime), which encodes each windows mean and standard deviation separately from its normalized shape. Interfaces / exposed object. magnitude-preserving global vector when level matters (amplitude is semantics); fixed-size patch embedding otherwise; the event-stream limit exposes historyconditioned state whose internal latent is not automatically an evaluated embedding. broadly adopted, retrieval-native frozen-encoder instrument is still missing. Arc. Features, kernels, and invariants (Era I) contrastive learning with the augmentation problem (Era II) patching and tokenization (Era III) foundation models and the LLM bridge (Era IV)four eras that, uniquely, have not cleanly superseded one another. Figure 14 summarizes 41 representative works. Modeling milestones. Distances, symbols, and shapes: DTW (Sakoe & Chiba, 1978), Takens (Takens, 1981), SAX (Lin et al., 2007), shapelets (Ye & Keogh, 2009), SAX-VSM (Senin & Malinchik, 2013) (tfidf-weighted SAX words as interpretable class vectors), BOSS (Schäfer, 2015) (bag-of-SFA-words histograms built to survive noise), Matrix Profile (Yeh et al., 2016) (exact all-pairs subsequence joins that unify motif, discord, and shapelet search), ROCKET (Dempster et al., 2020) Contrastive and invariant learning: T-Loss (Franceschi et al., 2019) (a triplet loss over sampled subwindows with dilated-convolution encoder), TS-TCC (Eldele et al., 2021) (temporal and contextual contrasting over two augmented views), TS2Vec (Yue et al., 2022), TF-C (Zhang et al., 2022b), T-Rep (Fraikin et al., 2024), MF-CLR (Duan et al., 2024), TimeHUT (Jalali et al., 2025), Series2Vec (Foumani et al., 2024) (predicting unsupervised series similarity instead of relying on augmentations), SOM-CPC (Huijben et al., 2023) (contrastive predictive coding tied 71 Omnimodal Embeddings to self-organizing-map codebook for high-rate sensor streams), DIVERSIFY (Lu et al., 2023c) (discovering latent sub-domains to learn out-of-distribution-robust representations) Patches, tokens, and post-attention encoders: PatchTST (Nie et al., 2023), TimeMAE (Cheng et al., 2026b) (a decoupled masked autoencoder combining masked codeword classification with masked representation regression), DLinear (Zeng et al., 2023), TSLANet (Eldele et al., 2024), NuTime (Lin et al., 2024) (magnitude preserving), hard-coded invariances (Germain et al., 2025), byte-pair encoding of series (Götz et al., 2025) Foundation models and the LLM bridge: MOMENT (Goswami et al., 2024), Chronos (Ansari et al., 2024), MOIRAI (Woo et al., 2024), TOTEM (Talukder et al., 2024), ROSE (Wang et al., 2025b), TimeDART (Wang et al., 2025a) (a causal patch encoder trained with diffusion loss in place of autoregressive MSE), TEST (Sun et al., 2024a), LETS-C (Kaur et al., 2025), aLLM4TS (Bian et al., 2024) Alignment and retrieval: TS-CLIP (Chen et al., 2025d), CLaSP (Ito et al., 2025), TimeRAG (Yang et al., 2025), TS-RAG (Ning et al., 2025) Event histories (temporal point processes): RMTPP (Du et al., 2016), Neural Hawkes (Mei & Eisner, 2017), SAHP (Zhang et al., 2020), THP (Zuo et al., 2020), Intensity-Free TPP (Shchur et al., 2020) (modeling conditional inter-event-time densities directly via normalizing flows and log-normal mixture with closed-form sampling and moments instead of an intensity function), A-NHP (Mei et al., 2022) (attention builds time-varying event and participant embeddings), Time2Vec (Kazemi et al., 2019) (a learnable, periodic representation of timestamp, used as drop-in time encoding), CoLES (Babaev et al., 2022), HCL-TPP (Wang et al., 2023b) (eventand sequence-level noise-contrastive estimation on top of maximum likelihood), MLEM (Yugay & Zaytsev, 2024) (masked event reconstruction combined with contrastive subsequence learning), CaRiNG (Chen et al., 2024a) (identifiable temporal causal representations under non-invertible generation), PromptTPP (Xue et al., 2023b) (a retrieval prompt pool that adapts neural TPPs to drifting streams), TPP-LLM (Liu & Quan, 2024) Evaluation benchmarks. The outlier: no broadly adopted frozen-encoder MTEB analog exists yet. Representation quality is instead reported as classification score probed on frozen encodings over the UCR univariate archive (Dau et al., 2019) and the UEA multivariate archive (Bagnall et al., 2018), or as end-to-end forecasting error on the Monash forecasting repository (Godahewa et al., 2021) and the recent GIFT-Eval (Aksu et al., 2024)the former controlled representation comparison, the latter joint property of encoder and forecast head. Cross-modal pointers. Continuous axis, no vocabulary, and magnitude semantics as the distinctive property (Section 9); the augmentation problem and declared-symmetry architectures (Section 3.1); serialization (LETS-C), discretization (Chronos), and rendering (VisionTS) as transformation (Section 6); continuous-time indexing and magnitude-preserving embedding as exports (Section 10); the missing broadly adopted frozen-encoder suite (Section 11). A.8 Other Modalities We review two additional families3D point cloud and biological sequencesmore compactly since they are more niche and their embedding literatures are younger. 3D / point cloud. point cloud is sparse, unordered set of samples over continuous surfacesan SE(3)-transformable geometric object rather than symbol sequence, so its structure is carried jointly by the input organization and the encoder architecture (Section 4.3). PointNet established the canonical interface: treat points as set, apply shared pointwise function, and aggregate with symmetric max-pool that makes the representation invariant to point order (Qi et al., 2017a); PointNet++ added hierarchical grouping and local aggregation over metric neighborhoods (Qi et al., 2017b). The self-supervised era then replayed the text recipe in miniature: Point-BERT masks point groups against learned discrete vocabulary and recovers them with BERT-style 72 Omnimodal Embeddings encoder (Yu et al., 2022b), Point-MAE masks points and regresses the missing coordinates with plain Transformer (Pang et al., 2022), and PointGPT moves to the generative corner, auto-regressively predicting point patches as GPT predicts tokens (Chen et al., 2023a). From there the family enters the same unification routes as every other modality: on the transformation path (Section 6), PointCLIP projects points into multi-view depth maps so pretrained visionlanguage model can read them directly (Zhang et al., 2022a); on the alignment path (Section 7), ULIP contrasts point clouds into the pretrained CLIP imagetext space (Xue et al., 2023a), OpenShape scales zero-shot 3D recognition over language descriptions (Liu et al., 2023b), and Uni3D pushes the point encoder itself to billion parameters (Zhou et al., 2024c). Evaluation, like time series, has no broadly adopted MTEB analog: representation quality is read out through trained heads on classification and part-segmentation suites and, on the alignment path, through zero-shot recognition in text-aligned space. Molecules and proteins. The biomolecular family pairs two data objects at very different scales: small molecules, whose atoms form either molecular graphs serializable as SMILES strings or 3D conformations with explicit atomic coordinates, and proteins, whose long amino-acid sequences read ever more like language. That is precisely what makes them interesting hereeach objective family of Part II has been run on them. The static word-vector analog is mol2vec, which trained word2vec verbatim over molecular substructures (Jaeger et al., 2018); year earlier, SchNet had replaced engineered fingerprints with continuous-filter message passing over atomic positions (Schütt et al., 2017). ChemBERTa then ran the BERT recipe directly on the SMILES string (Chithrananda et al., 2020), and GROVER scaled self-supervised graph pretraining to ten million molecules with hundredmillion-parameter model (Rong et al., 2020). On the protein side, ESM-2 showed that as protein language models grow, atomic-level structure emerges directly in the sequence embedding (Lin et al., 2023d)representation quality scaling with parameters, mirroring the scaling trajectory observed in vision at the molecular level. The alignment bridge follows the CLIP template as well: MoleculeSTM aligns molecular graphs with natural language (Liu et al., 2023c), and CLAMP pretrains molecules contrastively against assay descriptions (Seidl et al., 2023) (Section 7); the modality gap of Section 7.3 persists across very different modality pairs, amino-acid sequence encoders included (Liang et al., 2022). Evaluation again runs through task headsproperty prediction for molecules, structure and function prediction for proteinswith no embedding-native benchmark on the horizon yet (Section 11). Omnimodal Embeddings

sections.title: B Quantitative Analysis of the Literature
sections.content: This section grounds three claims of the main text in simple bibliometric evidence: that embedding research is timely (i.e., the object of study is growing, not receding), that it remains fragmented across communities (Section 1.1), and that early signals of cross-modal convergence are measurable at the level of publication venue and terminology. Two views are used: title-term baseline over arXiv metadata for 20152025, and manually curated census of formally published conference and journal papers for 20232025. B.1 An arXiv title-term analysis (20152025) Method. For each year from 2015 to 2025, we queried the arXiv API for every record in cs.CL, cs.CV, eess.AS, cs.LG, cs.IR, and cs.DB (i.e., the main categories for text, vision, audio processing and other major embedding modalities) whose title matches the keyword embedding or representation learning. Among the matches, 767 records whose only match is spurious stem (typically embedded devices or embedded systems) and 87 records whose sole use of the word embedding is inside position-embedding-style phrase (e.g., positional encoding with rotary position embeddings) are removed. This leaves 10,952 records out of 11,806 candidates. Findings. Figure 15 shows the resulting findings. First, the field is large and mostly mature: kept records grow from 140 in 2015 to 1,784 in 2025, but growth has slowedthe union count increased by 13% from 2024 to 2025, against 73% single-year jump from 2018 to 2019and eess.AS remains an order of magnitude smaller than the three largest categories, consistent with the minority position of speech noted in this paper. Second, the center of gravity has moved: cs.CL peaked in 2019 (432) and was overtaken by cs.CV in 2021, which reached 550 in 2025; both trail cs.LGthe general machinelearning category and the largest of the six since 2018, at 952 records in 2025while cs.IR grows steadily to 187 and cs.DB stays marginal. Third, and most relevant to our argument, multimodal keyword families behave very differently on this slow-moving baseline: titles containing multimodal embedding (representation learning is counted as synonym of embedding) never exceed ten per year before 2023, then rise to 15, 29, and 62 in 20232025a 2.1 single-year jump from 2024 to 2025, against the 13% total growthbringing their share of embedding-titled records from roughly 1% or less for most of the decade to 3.5% in 2025. The cross-modal embedding family, by contrast, never exceeds eight titles per year across the whole window. In other words, the vocabulary that names the object of this surveya unified multimodal embedding spaceis expanding, and it is expanding specifically on the multimodal side rather than through pairwise cross-modal phrasing. Figure 15: arXiv title-term analysis, 20152025. Left: yearly counts of arXiv records containing the keyword embedding or representation learning in cs.CL, cs.CV, eess.AS, cs.LG, cs.IR, and cs.DB (i.e., text, vision, audio, machine learning, information retrieval, and databases). Right: comparison between all embedding papers and those containing the keyword multimodal embedding and cross-modal embedding. Omnimodal Embeddings B.2 curated census of conference papers (20232025) Method. The second view covers works published at peer-reviewed venues. We manually collected and classified papers on embedding and representation learning across nine modality buckets (text, code, vision, audio, graph, time series, recommendation, others, and cross-modal alignment as deliberately cross-cutting bucket), from the major venues of the different communities: the NLP conferences (ACL, EMNLP, NAACL), the vision conferences (CVPR, ICCV, ECCV, ACM MM), the speech conferences (InterSpeech, ICASSP), the ML conferences (ICLR, NeurIPS, ICML, and TMLR), and IR and related venues (SIGIR, WWW, KDD, TPAMI). Findings. Figure 16 shows the venue matrix and yearly totals. The fragmentation claimed in Section 1 is directly visible as structure: text embeddings live overwhelmingly in the NLP conferences (237 of 308), audio embeddings in the two speech conferences (309 of 334), and recommendation at SIGIR, while vision, graph, and time series spread across the ML conferencesICLR, NeurIPS, and ICML alone host 205 of the 386 vision-bucket papers. Meanwhile the cross-cutting bucket behaves unlike any of them: cross-modal alignment papers are concentrated at CVPR (48 of 66) and the bucket is the only one that roughly doubles twice in succession, from 7 to 22 to 37 collected papers across 20232025. Speech is also the only bucket in visible retreat (13612078), while remaining the most venue-isolated. These observations are consistent with the arXiv analysis above: the communities are siloed by venue precisely where they are largest, and the fastest-growing published work is the work that crosses modality boundaries. Figure 16: Curated conference and journal papers on embedding and representation learning, 20232025 (1,352 formally published papers across nine modality buckets). Left: modality venue matrix, pooled over the three years; the last Others column includes SIGIR, WWW, KDD, and TPAMI. Right: yearly totals per bucket, with cross-modal alignment highlighted: 7 22 37, the fastest-growing bucket in the census while most buckets are flat or declining. B.3 Limitations Both views are deliberately narrow, and we state their limitations here so their evidence is not over-read. (i) The queries are phrase-based: they exclude neighboring terminologies (e.g., unified representation space), so all counts are lower bounds for the family of interest rather than accurate estimates of it. (ii) Title-level matching biases the sample toward work that signals its subject in the title; methodological work that uses embeddings without naming them is invisible. (iii) The counts only measure where the fields attention sits, how siloed its publishing venues remain, and which corner of the literature is growing fastestnot whether any particular embedding construction preserves complementary information, models cross-modal interactions, or improves downstream reasoning. Those questions require the controlled evidence surveyed in the main text. 75 Omnimodal Embeddings
